#173150. Latest Update: Comment | The future of the ancient city of Palmyra should be determined by its local community

Latest Update: Comment | The future of the ancient city of Palmyra should be determined by its local community

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ancient city of Palmyra in Syria rose to the world’s attention in May 2015, when Isis militants occupied the site.
  • In the wake of these atrocities, institutions and governments around the globe introduced a dizzying array of projects.
  • Now under a newly introduced government, the Syrian antiquities department’s efforts to restore Palmyra—a Unesco World Heritage Site since 1980—are again progressing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ancient city of Palmyra in Syria rose to the world’s attention in May 2015, when Isis militants occupied the site. Within five months, they had destroyed the Temple of Baalshamin, the Temple of Bel, and the Arch of Triumph—all 2,000-year-old masterpieces. That same year, their murder of Khaled al-Asaad, Palmyra’s retired head of antiquities, sparked worldwide outrage.

In the wake of these atrocities, institutions and governments around the globe introduced a dizzying array of projects. Many focused on preserving the site digitally: the University of California San Diego Library reconstructed the Temple of Bel, for example, and the Université de Lausanne did likewise for the Temple of Baalshamin. Others aimed to one day physically reconstruct what had been lost, including a Russian project to restore the Arch of Triumph. But by the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, none of these prepares had been realised.

Now under a newly introduced government, the Syrian antiquities department’s efforts to restore Palmyra—a Unesco World Heritage Site since 1980—are again progressing. It has been working to remove illegal constructions and stop illegal excavations, while Palmyra’s local community has been engaged in cleaning the museum’s gardens, among other projects. Meanwhile, a Heritage for Peace project is evaluating the structural condition of buildings in Palmyra’s modern city, which had a pre-war population of 70,000. This renewed momentum once again raises an important question: to what extent should Palmyra’s ancient ruins be physically reconstructed, if at all?

Archaeologist Nour A. Munawar of the University of Amsterdam addressed this problem in 2017, while the war still raged. He emphasised that whether or not to reconstruct should be a decision for Palmyra’s local community, irrespective of where they now live or their political views. Writing in Ex Noxo Journal of Archaeology, he warns that previous reconstruction projects largely left communities out of discussions—such as the limited local consultation when the Stari Most bridge was rebuilt in Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or how commercial buildings dominated the reconstruction of post-war Beirut. There is also the danger of “Disneyfication”, a label for artificial, over-polished reconstructions.

In a recent development, whether to reconstruct has long been a dilemma for war-ravaged places. I recently visited Ypres, Belgium, a city that was totally destroyed during the First World War. In the aftermath, some wondered whether it should be rebuilt as it once appeared, or if its old architecture should be replaced with something more modern. Winston Churchill was in favour of leaving it untouched, as a memorial to the horrors of war. In the end, the local people made the decision: they wanted their Medieval town rebuilt—even if, for the most part, only the facades reflected the pre-war era.

Industry observers note that A 2024 study by Benjamin Isakhan, a professor of international politics at Deakin University, Melbourne, and Lynn Meskell, a professor of anthropology at the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, provides an insight into how Syrians feel about this concern. After surveying 1,600 Aleppo residents, they found that almost all were proud of their cultural heritage, but Aleppines prioritised “safety and security”, “electricity, water and other services” and “unemployment and poverty” over “heritage protection and reconstruction” in terms of urgency.

And although 98% agreed that damaged or destroyed heritage sites should be restored or reconstructed, opinions varied on how: 17% wanted them to appear as “first built”, 24% as they appeared before the war, and 30% wanted them “restored and reconstructed into a new and more modern structure”. Heritage experts’ preference for authenticity could therefore go against some local wishes. Overwhelmingly, Aleppines also wanted Syrian control over rebuilding their heritage, not global agencies, NGOs, and foreign governments, Isakhan and Meskell note in the International Journal of Heritage Studies.

Industry observers note that palmyra is now a symbol of Syria, known worldwide. But whether the city’s rebuilt heritage retains its battle scars, becomes “Disneyfied”, or something in between, should be a local choice, as should whether any reconstruction is prioritised over more pressing needs. As time passes, an increasing number of voices will come into play—the fresh Syrian government, foreign governments, international bodies, NGOs and cultural heritage experts—all providing much-needed money, aid and advice. We must hope that the local community is not lost in the mix. In the end, it must be the people of Palmyra who decide their city’s fate.

Graphaselâs packaging design for Kontyos Don Cherry Vermut breaks aperitif clichÃ©s with ribbed cherry-red type on a die-cut turquoise label.

One repeating vertical stripe ties this whole bottle together. Look closely at Hungarian studio Graphaselâs work for Kontyos Don Cherry Vermut, and the rhythm shows up in three places at once. Fine vertical fluting runs straight down the heavy crimson DON letters, mirrors the red-and-white striped wrap on the screw-cap neck, and returns on the illustrated characterâs open-collared shirt. According to the studioâs project notes, the goal was a bold, youthful identity that leaves traditional vermouth codes behind in favor of summer warmth and contemporary drinking culture. It doesnât lean on antique engravings or ornate crest borders to signal heritage. Saturated turquoise paper wraps a broad-shouldered, short-necked dark glass bottle built for an afternoon patio table.

The flat macro plate of the standalone label exposes how much tactile craft sits inside that two-tone palette. Pebbled turquoise paper curves into a soft arch at the top to cradle the white KONTYOS header, then breaks out of its rectangular frame at the bottom right. That contoured die-cut edge traces the lounging figureâs flared coral-red trouser cuff and boot, giving the front of the bottle an unmistakable physical silhouette. Above the illustration, chunky cherry-red DON capitals pack tightly side to side, punctuated by a tiny circular counter perched high inside the O. Crisp white CHERRY lettering sits directly below, flanked by small volume specs and tracked-out red VERMUT type â while the reclining figureâs raised coupe glass cuts into the right edge of the wordmark so character and typography lock into one unit.

Across the photography, the packaging design stays disciplined about color and mood. On a sunlit stone ledge beside turquoise pool water, the bottle stands behind a metallic-red portable radio and three cherry cocktails casting crisp caustics across the surface. Elsewhere, hands raise a chilled rocks glass beside the bottle against a cyan backdrop, and an overhead flat-lay nests the dark glass directly into wet cherries and melting ice cubes. Even the outdoor shot perched on a sun-faded turquoise vintage car fender extends the same red-and-teal pairing without adding a single stray prop color. That packaging design focus keeps a playful 1970s attitude looking sharp from every angle.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is our largest (and most fun) Film Friday of the year: Black (and White) Film Friday!
  • According to recent reports, this story is brought to you by Blue Moon Camera and Machine in Portland, OR.
  • PetaPixel Members receive 10% off all lab services with Blue Moon: Join today!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is our largest (and most fun) Film Friday of the year: Black (and White) Film Friday! While our Film Fridays tend to spotlight a single emulsion, with this annual celebration we feature the entire selection of black and white film stocks that we have in our inventory. But before we dig in too far, it would be a good moment to explain our inspiration for Film Friday.

According to recent reports, this story is brought to you by Blue Moon Camera and Machine in Portland, OR. Blue Moon offers film, development services, printing, and even an ever-rotating line of film cameras and lenses.

PetaPixel Members receive 10% off all lab services with Blue Moon: Join today!

In a recent development, blue Moon Camera and Machine launched Film Friday publicly in 2019, but it had been an ongoing project of ours for several years prior to that. The film that started it all was Ilford XP2. See, we (the collective “we”, that is, as in all of us film photographers) have always had an amazing selection of films to choose from as we decide what to load in our cameras. This selection has evolved over time. Some years it has winnowed down, and other years it has actually expanded. But there have always been just so many films out there to make our work and art with. It is also true, however, that most of us gravitate to certain films. We find the emulsion we like, and we settle into it.

In a recent development, this is neither a good behavior nor a bad one—perhaps it is both; it is simply what we tend to do. And even when you work in an all-analog camera store, like Blue Moon Camera, you can fall into these patterns. And this is where XP2 comes in. Ilford XP2 was one of those films we never used all that much. To be honest, Kodak Tri-X and Ilford HP5 were our typical go-to film stocks. Yet every now and then we would find cause to shoot with a roll of XP2 instead.

It has been revealed that this might happen two or three times a year. And each of those times we would get the negatives back and think to ourselves, “Wow, XP2 is a gorgeous film. Why don’t we use this stuff more often?” Of course, the answer is because we know what we know, and we like to stick with that. And thus we decided to set about changing this. We made it a personal project to not just shoot a roll of every film we carried, but actually use it repeatedly and get to know it. One film at a time we would go out for several months, working through multiple rolls, taking our time, learning each emulsion’s quirks and characteristics, and then coalescing those experiences into a collection of images and a written review. The goal was to pass along not just the knowledge and experience we had gained, but the inspiration as well.

In a recent development, there is something to be said for working in depth and committing to a single film and knowing it like you know nothing else. But there is also something to be said about breadth and being familiar with all the myriad options open to you in your creative pursuits. And that is the beating heart of our Film Fridays. It is about celebrating the wealth of options open to us. It is about reminding ourselves that there are more films out there than simply Ultramax, Portra, or HP5. And of course, it is about learning and growing as film photographers.

In a recent development, so having noted all that, we came up with the idea of Black (and White) Film Friday only a few years ago. Yes, it is timed to coincide with Black Friday, and yes, quite admittedly, there is a bit of a commercial gimmick built into that. But there is also more to our B&W Film Friday than the sales angle. Let us explain.

In a similar way to how many of us gravitate toward a select few film stocks, we have also noticed that, generally speaking, many film photographers lean toward color film photography. This is especially true with newer film photographers. A substantial reason is we see the world, and our lives, in color, so it is a natural or even reflexive deduction to photograph with color film. Time and again we have had customers at the counter ask for film recommendations, and we, in turn, ask if they are interested in color or B&W film. It is not uncommon for them to respond to that simple question with some surprise that they had not even considered black and white and had never even tried a roll of it. This is the thing with habits; they tend to fit so snugly we can forget they are even there.

Sources indicate that but B&W film should not be forgotten or overlooked. In short, there is a classic beauty and a timelessness that can only be captured with B&W film. It also simplifies the world in its way by converting colors that may otherwise be distracting into tones of grey and letting us make images about something other than the reds, oranges, yellows, greens, blues, and violets of the world.

Black and white allows us to focus on light, textures, relationships, shapes, patterns, grit, grain, and so many other elements (or ideas). It isn’t that you cannot do these things with color film—you can—but there is a directness with which B&W lets you approach these things. This is harder to understand via explanation than it is through experience. So we run our B&W Film Friday not just for the photographers who already love their black and white films, but also for those who have never stepped into those waters.

Industry observers note that and there is a crazy variety out there to work with. There are more different types of black and white films than there are color films. We did a rough count, and once you eliminate all the different format choices and focus on just the different emulsions, we have at least 45 unique film stocks to try.

Industry observers note that these films are mostly of the black and white negative type, but there are a few reversal films as well and also a couple of black and white instant films to keep in mind. Let’s repeat that number for emphasis: there are at least 45 unique black and white films in our inventory alone. And we don’t even carry every possible B&W film option on the market. That is easily in the 50s and maybe the 60s once you go out into the wider market looking for these films.

According to recent reports, so what are you waiting for? That is a lot of film to try, and our guess is most of you have perhaps not even used half of these. So take advantage of this one day where you can pick up more of your favorite B&W film, or you can try something entirely fresh. We heartily recommend doing both. Visit our online store or come by our shop in St. Johns, Portland, Oregon, and get some film.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production tech giant Sturdy.
  • The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.
  • To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production tech giant Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he noted.

“His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between reveals across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

“That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time highlights were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he mentioned.

“We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent indicates at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mucho's Biotic brand identity grows from a single dot into a living system, turning one synthetic cell into many through reaction-diffusion.
  • Biotic is a nonprofit stewarding SpudCell, a synthetic cell built from scratch rather than modified from an existing one.
  • Industry observers note that the wordmark pairs the dot with lowercase biotic in Roobert Medium, the primary typeface, with Medium as the default weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mucho's Biotic brand identity grows from a single dot into a living system, turning one synthetic cell into many through reaction-diffusion.

Biotic is a nonprofit stewarding SpudCell, a synthetic cell built from scratch rather than modified from an existing one. Mucho answers that science with a mark as plain as the idea behind it: one black dot, the simplest shape a single cell can take. From that dot the identity grows. Reaction-diffusion software built by Karl Sims lets the pattern branch, split and multiply across every surface, so the same dot that opens the website also fills a stage screen, a tote bag and a stack of business cards. Black and white carry the whole system, with a lime accent kept for small moments like the arrow buttons on the site.

Industry observers note that the wordmark pairs the dot with lowercase biotic in Roobert Medium, the primary typeface, with Medium as the default weight. Headlines run large and plain, often as a single statement across a page: Out of one, many. on a phone screen, Building the Operating System for Accessible Biology on the community page. Dotted rules divide sections instead of solid lines, a quiet nod to cells lining up in a row. The grid stays open and calm, with wide black fields and white panels trading places down the page.

Sources indicate that the system proves itself on paper and cloth. Business cards stack in a grid, each one carrying a different reaction-diffusion circle and the line Out of one, many. Three black booklets carry white circles and three short lines: Propagating possibility. Building biology. Honoring Humanity. A white tote prints one large circle under the small dot wordmark. The guidelines show the next phase too, with the same circles in blue, green and purple, color held back until the science is ready for it. On the website, a live clock counts down to 2050, the year Biotic calls Bloomsday, when the world may no longer produce enough resources for its growing population.

See more from Mucho on their website.

  • Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) (1934) by Mark Rothko.
  • In a recent development, christopher Rothko, the son of the artist Mark Rothko (1903-70), states that while his father thought “all art was inherently of its time”, sometimes “even with a master of abstraction like Mark Rothko, art can also be inherently of its place”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

National Gallery of Australia, Canberra.

The American Friends of the National Gallery of Australia bought this sculpture by Simone Leigh last year from Matthew Marks Gallery in New York. The monumental bronze, measuring 3.3m long and 1.5m tall, is named after the Nigerian American artist and actress Okwui Okpokwasili. It shows a reclining woman in a cast raffia skirt, exploring the resilience and cultural memory that merges the semi-abstract female form with the African vernacular. This cast is the second from an edition of two (with one artist’s proof). In 2022, Leigh became the first Black woman to represent the US at the Venice Biennale.

Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) (1934) by Mark Rothko.

Cape Ann Museum/Christopher Rothko.

Cape Ann Museum, Gloucester, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, christopher Rothko, the son of the artist Mark Rothko (1903-70), states that while his father thought “all art was inherently of its time”, sometimes “even with a master of abstraction like Mark Rothko, art can also be inherently of its place”. He is referring to this painting—an atmospheric early watercolour-and-gouache work depicting the harbour in Gloucester—which Christopher recently donated to the Cape Ann Museum from his private collection. Mark Rothko frequently summered on Cape Ann, painting alongside two other Upcoming York artists: his mentor, Milton Avery, and his friend Adolph Gottlieb. This painting is included in Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea—a touring exhibition at the moment on view at the Phillips Collection in Washington, DC (until 24 January 2027).

Recent findings suggest that arc-en-ciel no. 5 (1913-14) by Robert Delaunay.

Recent findings suggest that it may not be instantly recognisable, but the lilac spire behind the rainbow in this painting is the Eiffel Tower—the tallest building in the world when the work was painted by Robert Delaunay (1885-1941). The French artist was the husband of Sonia Delaunay, and in 1912 they co-founded the short-lived Orphism movement—an offshoot of Cubism that prized bright colours and geometric shapes. This vivid oil-on-canvas work, measuring 35cm by 40cm, is one of several variations of the composition and reveals Delaunay moving away from strict geometry to a looser, more expressive and rhythmic style. The painting, which sold at Christie’s in 2025 for $317,500 (with fees) from the collection of Arnold and Joan Saltzman, was exhibited by the London-based dealer Willoughby Gerrish at Tefaf Maastricht in March—where the sale to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, was initially agreed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Nikon D850 may be on its last legs, but that doesn’t mean photographers can no longer get their hands on one.
  • Nikon Rumors reports that Nikon’s Sales Support team in the United Kingdom communicated that the Nikon D850 is “now end of life,” which effectively means it is discontinued.
  • “We would like to inform you that the D850 model is now end of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nikon D850 may be on its last legs, but that doesn’t mean photographers can no longer get their hands on one.

Nikon Rumors reports that Nikon’s Sales Support team in the United Kingdom communicated that the Nikon D850 is “now end of life,” which effectively means it is discontinued.

“We would like to inform you that the D850 model is now end of life. Unfortunately, we are not expecting any further stock, and as a result, we are not accepting new orders. Please revision your systems accordingly. We apologize for any inconvenience. If you have any questions, please let us know,” Nikon’s UK Sales Team remarked in an email.

According to recent reports, this aligns with the UK retail situation, where stock varies by retailer. For example, Wex, a major UK photo retailer, no longer lists the D850. However, as Digicame-Info reports, the D850 is still available in Japan, and it remains easy to find in the United States as well.

There are a couple of caveats here. First, as PetaPixel has seen plenty of times, cameras and lenses are often discontinued in one region before another. Second, nothing may have actually changed regarding Nikon’s manufacturing of the D850. The company could have halted production a while ago, and local stock has only just run dry in the UK, prompting the newly introduced notice.

PetaPixel has reached out to Nikon for clarification and will upgrade this story when more information becomes available.

Sources indicate that in the meantime, photographers can still acquire the Nikon D850. Even if upcoming stock runs out, this prolific DSLR is widely available on the used market.

In a recent development, as for brand-upcoming units, they remain readily available in the United States. B&H still carries the Nikon D850, for instance, and has it discounted by $300 through November 29 for the holidays. Nikon USA also still sells the D850 directly.

The Nikon D850 remains a fantastic camera that photographers still love, and it will stay easy to buy for the foreseeable future. The only real question is how much longer it will be available brand-new in the box—a status that will eventually end everywhere, not just in the UK.

PGYTECH RetroVa Gives the iPhone a 400mm Reach and a Real Camera Feel

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that PGYTECH is best known for camera bags, tripods and straps, and in the phone world for telephoto extender lenses designed for Vivo and Oppo flagships.
  • Industry observers note that the system first appeared on Kickstarter in January 2026 for the iPhone 16 Pro and 17 Pro families, combining a camera-style Bluetooth grip, retro-style case, and a 2.35x teleconverter for the phone’s telephoto lens.
  • This all provides focal range that simply doesn’t work as well when using the phone itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that PGYTECH is best known for camera bags, tripods and straps, and in the phone world for telephoto extender lenses designed for Vivo and Oppo flagships. Its RetroVa kit brings that lens work to the iPhone.

Industry observers note that the system first appeared on Kickstarter in January 2026 for the iPhone 16 Pro and 17 Pro families, combining a camera-style Bluetooth grip, retro-style case, and a 2.35x teleconverter for the phone’s telephoto lens. The newest version designed for the iPhone 17 Pro/Pro Max and 18 Pro/Pro Max series brings in a lighter and smaller 2X lens, along with a 4X telephoto lens as an alternative.

This all provides focal range that simply doesn’t work as well when using the phone itself. With 200mm, 235mm, and 400mm equivalents, the iPhone can reach farther with more optical clarity. A dedicated app also offers old school film simulations and manual controls for composition to let you decide how you want your images to look.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set comes in Graphite Black, while the 4X lens, grip, and the case are also sold separately and in smaller bundles, offering people different ways to put the kit together.

RetroVa Black Friday deal: From November 19 to 30, the RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set (Graphite Black, iPhone 17/18 Pro Max) is 10% off, and PetaPixel readers can take an extra 10% off with code BYTEDDYK. Buy it on Amazon or directly from PGYTECH.

The Ultimate Gift Set brings them all together in the box: the 4X telephoto lens, a lens adapter bracket, lens pouch, RetroVa phone case, grip, a photography strap, and an Arca-Swiss compatible tripod collar for the lens. The case is polycarbonate and works with MagSafe, leaving the proverbial door open for additional magnetic accessories. Though it has a lip over the edges, you can still use the case with a screen protector on the phone itself.

The lightweight grip weighs 63 grams for the Pro and 65.4 grams for the Pro Max. It carries physical controls, a built-in microSD slot, and a standard 1/4-inch socket on the base for tripods and monopods. It slides into the phone’s USB-C port with a lock switch that holds it firmly in place, though it actually pairs and connects to the device via Bluetooth.

In a recent development, it’s important to get the right size because there are separate variants for the Pro and Pro Max. While the lens mount is the same on either build, you can’t slide a Pro grip into the Pro Max, for instance. That also goes for the case, which is the most integral piece because that’s what everything else in the kit attaches to. Fortunately, since the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro models share the same dimensions, you don’t need to worry about compatibility in that regard.

It has been revealed that the shutter button functions a lot like a typical camera would: half-press to focus, press to take the shot, or hold it down for a burst. The zoom lever right under it can either skip between focal lengths in Vintage mode or adjust zoom more freely in the Standard setting. Below that is the control dial that you can choose to adjust exposure, ISO, white balance, or shutter speed. Lastly, the multi-function button acts as power on/off, switches modes, and sets up Bluetooth pairing. A small LED next to it indicates pairing and a solid connection.

The microSD card slot (UHS-I or UHS-II) underneath is another handy way to save excess photos or video, albeit with some key parameters. You can readily save RAW photos or 4K video to it, only you’re limited to HEVC-coded footage and max 120fps. Plug the grip into a laptop where you can then offload the content directly.

In a recent development, if you record in Apple’s Camera app, video automatically goes to the card when you use supported formats, while PGYTECH’s app supports more recording formats. Even third-party apps that can record to external storage can recognize the card, too.

Industry observers note that PGYTECH also makes 62mm and 67mm filter adapter rings sold separately from the available kits. They’re not included in any of them, though will work just fine with any filters in those two respective sizes. Being a separate piece, you just slide out the lens adapter ring and bring in the filter adapter instead. There is no way to use a filter with the teleconverter lenses themselves, since the filter adapter covers the iPhone’s entire rear array.

Industry observers note that PGYTECH designed the kit to work with a dedicated companion app called PGYTECH: Pro Camera & Editor. It’s free to download, only requiring iOS 17 or later to run. You do, however, need to be diligent about keeping it up to date because if you don’t, the app may lock you out of all the manual control settings. A pop-up notice stating that a subscription is required to unlock those pro features isn’t actually necessary. Update the app and that message disappears.

Industry observers note that while there is an Auto mode available, Manual provides controls for exposure, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, tint, and filters, which you can then map to the grip by going to Settings->Hardware Settings. You will need to ensure the grip is on and once connected via Bluetooth, select RetroVa in the drop-down menu to pick what you want. At any point within that section, you can always look at tutorials on connecting the grip and a video FAQ as well.

Industry observers note that unless you explicitly make your own manual adjustments, the app’s camera interface treats everything as if it was in Auto. So, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, and tint will all dynamically shift based on what’s in frame. Tap to focus works just like any other camera app would. One difference, though, is if you have Focus Assist on (focus peaking by another name), you will see where the camera is actually focusing after you tap, giving you an indication of where the focal plane is.

Other manual controls, like a histogram and priority facial recognition (the camera will always focus on a face first in this setting), are elective. Standard bits, like a timer, live photo, watermark, and aspect ratio (1:1, 4:3, and 16:9) round out much of what’s left. There is a Dive Mode that switches controls to physical buttons for underwater photos and video, while also applying an “underwater filter” as a copy of the original when captured. You can make separate manual settings adjustments for this mode, too.

According to recent reports, in addition to about 15 standard filters, PGYTECH offers a series of nostalgic film simulations, ranging from Classic Negative and Nostalgic Negative to Kodak Gold 200, Fujifilm PRO Neg Std, Velvia 100, Classic Chrome, FujiColor C200, Tungsten 500, and Bleach Bypass. Choose any one at any time and adjust the intensity from 0-100. These simulations apply no matter what image format you shoot with and aren’t limited to still photos: they work with video, too.

According to recent reports, the app includes a Retro Film mode that features the same set of film simulations, except it changes the hybrid zoom ranges to include 35mm and 50mm equivalents to better match traditional prime lenses. Otherwise, images process the same way as the Photo mode.

According to recent reports, it’s also possible to apply any of these filters on a photo after you capture it within the in-app editing suite, including HSL for some color grading. Beauty features also present a variety of options for those seeking that kind of detail. Under Creative, there are templates for sharing or social media.

An on-device AI tool in the Adjust section lets you try enhancing detail in images by either using HD to improve clarity or AI HD to restore detail in softer images. You need to download it to make it work on-device rather than in the cloud but once it’s there, you can utilize it any time. If you’d rather avoid AI completely, you don’t have to use it.

Sources indicate that mind you, you’re not forced into PGYTECH’s app for basic shooting (without the lenses) since the grip also works with the native Camera app. To make that work with iOS, go to the Settings app, then Accessibility->Zoom->toggle On->Full Screen Zoom. At that point, having already paired it to the phone, you gain access to Apple’s own Camera app where pressing the shutter or zooming in responds onscreen. PGYTECH says it’s working on more third-party app integrations, so we’ll see where that leads.

It has been revealed that the 4X lens is both the newest and the headline of the trio. It uses an 11-element, 3-group optical design with fluorite-grade low-dispersion glass and weighs about 137 grams. It feels sturdy in hand, which is why it’s smart to use it with the tripod collar when you need to prop it up for a long exposure or timelapse.

It has been revealed that it’s a 400mm equivalent optical focal length, going up to 1200mm with a digital crop. The 4x lens also comes with a case and slightly different bracket that also includes a mount for the iPhone’s main camera. That gives you a 240mm optical equivalent or 400mm with an in-sensor crop with more background separation, which PGYTECH pitches for portraits.

It has been revealed that the 2x lens, at about 104 grams, gives 200mm optical and 400mm cropped over the telephoto camera, or 105mm and 200mm over the main camera. This lens doesn’t come with a case but does include the same lens bracket the Ultimate Gift Set does, which only covers the phone’s telephoto camera. That’s an notable distinction if you’re looking to use any of the lenses on both the main and telephoto cameras.

Industry observers note that in the case of the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the PGYTECH app can’t control the main camera’s mechanical aperture, so you can’t benefit from stopping down to f/4 for certain photo or video opportunities. Either way, all three lenses fit any of the RetroVa cases and brackets made for the iPhone.

It has been revealed that one thing to always keep in mind is how much attaching the lenses considerably increases minimum focusing distance. PGYTECH lists 16.2 meters for the 4x over the telephoto camera and three meters over the main camera, against 5.22 meters and 60 centimeters for the 2x. There’s no optical image stabilization in any of them, so PGYTECH relies on its app’s stabilization algorithm for steadier handheld results. Handheld, the kit is better now than it was just a few months ago.

There’s nothing electronic communicating between the lenses and the app, so you have to manually select the lens you’re using and then turn that off or switch if you end up putting on another one. Doing so makes corresponding changes to available focal lengths and ensures focusing and processing fall in line with what you’re using. It’s one of the easiest things to forget while shooting with it in the field but it’s vitally important.

In a recent development, technically, the lenses aren’t supposed to work with Apple’s own app, though I randomly found no obstruction in doing so. Other times, it didn’t work at all. This has nothing to do with the kit and everything to do with how Apple engineers its camera array. Because it functions as one virtual system, the software can decide what it thinks is the best camera, even though you’ve already chosen one over another. PGYTECH’s app doesn’t do that, leaning purely on whichever camera you’ve attached the lens to capture images or video.

Industry observers note that if you get lucky enough to make Apple’s app work, it gives you access to manual controls (in the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max) as well as the possibility of manipulating the variable aperture with the main camera. It’s just a very hit-or-miss proposition, so your experience may truly vary.

Recent findings suggest that as a kit, the RetroVa is trying to present a camera-like feel to capturing photos and video on the iPhone. That’s the basic gist, but in practice, the handling offers a fairly high degree of versatility in both perspective and ergonomics. Without having to stretch out a thumb or finger to hit the onscreen shutter, the grip’s controls make low or high-angle shots easier to manage. Double-clicking the iPhone’s Camera Control will launch Apple’s Camera app but if you prefer to switch that to PGYTECH’s app within iOS, go to Settings->Camera->Camera Control and tap on it to make that the default.

In the four months I’ve been using the kit (both with the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro), multiple updates over that time have either added new features or refined existing ones. One thing you have to always remember is that this app processes images slower than Apple’s app does, especially when shooting in ProRAW. You can see that in the preview window where a yellow indicator shows that it’s rendering what you just shot.

The reason that matters is because it’s easy to ruin a photo by promptly moving the camera after capture. That very brief window between snapping the shutter and seeing the resulting image populate the preview window can feel like an eternity when shooting action, like I did at multiple WNBA games with this kit. It’s faster if you’re purely shooting JPEG or HEIF but the same thing can happen if you’re a little too eager to see what you just got.

According to recent reports, part of what PGYTECH is up against is the smaller 1/2.55-inch sensor Apple uses for the telephoto camera on both the 17 Pro and 18 Pro series. Adding significant optics to that lens certainly gets you closer to the subject or action but it’s best to also learn the subtleties of PGYTECH’s app. Lighting conditions are of paramount importance, as noise can creep in at higher ISO levels when you need to raise the shutter speed.

In a recent development, while you can shoot in either ProRAW, JPEG, or HEIF at either 12 or 48-megapixels, you don’t really wield any outsized control over the imaging pipeline. Apple’s processing engine still kicks in, forcing you to lean more on RAW images if you feel more comfortable with the higher degree of manual control available. PGYTECH isn’t necessarily only targeting seasoned mobile photographers with the RetroVa kit but it’s still worth dealing with the learning curve.

It has been revealed that the controls include manual focus, with focus peaking as an elective option where you get to choose between red, green, or blue as the visual aid. It applies no matter if you’re tapping to focus manually or adjusting it in the slider. One key tidbit is tapping to focus doesn’t always work as you’d expect because focal length (even for the iPhone’s own lenses) behave natively. Within the app, there’s no fusion between them to enable, say, macro shooting at closer distances where the main or ultra-wide might step in to help the cause.

In a recent development, all that aside, the handling is a major part of the appeal here. As a slab device, the iPhone can prove tough to work with under different perspective and angles, so the grip turns it into something you can maneuver in more interesting ways. With a finger on the shutter and the ability to make granular adjustments with the dial, plus the strap to take off the weight, the creative possibilities certainly stand out.

Focusing is the biggest challenge because subject tracking isn’t the same as Apple’s own implementation, and you often still need to tap on the screen to hone in on what you want the composition to look like. One workaround for that is to get a separate screen primarily used for rear camera selfies as a way to wirelessly compose a shot when it’s hard to contort yourself to see the real time preview on the phone.

It has been revealed that PGYTECH notes it’s working on tracking autofocus and on controlling the iPhone’s aperture from the grip, which would address two key challenges in using the RetroVa kit. A universal lens adapter and further lens types are also on PGYTECH’s wish list, though no firm commitment.

For now, RetroVa is an iPhone-only system built around the Pro and Pro Max models, albeit with some nuances noted earlier. Not everything made for the iPhone 17 and 18 Pro series applies to what’s available for the iPhone 16 Pro series.

It has been revealed that it’s also worth noting the kit isn’t a qualitative replacement for a mirrorless camera. The iPhone’s image sensors aren’t in the same league to begin with, but the app’s manual controls are far more extensive and the lenses a massive upgrade over the awful hybrid crops the iPhone offers on its own. Compared to a bigger mirrorless, however, this kit is easier to carry, especially when you take off the lenses.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set is 10% off through November 30, plus an extra 10% with code BYTEDDYK, on Amazon and at PGYTECH.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.
  • Specifically, he noted he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he noted he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

It has been revealed that “Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he said he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

Industry observers note that it also proposes latest legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

Sources indicate that “I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

Sources indicate that “While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

Yoto is presently up to 30% off – and it would make a fabulous Christmas present.

If you're thinking about a console for your children this Christmas, I really can't recommend this one enough – and it's also currently got 37% in the UK, and 30% in the US off for Black Friday.

My daughter is on the borderline at 9, but my son (5) would get plenty of life from this printer.

In a recent development, it's a fun design, and is super-simple to use via an app. You can draw designs and let the AI print them, or pick from a marketplace of designs (make sure you use the official UGEE designs for maximum effectiveness). Because it's enclosed, it's safer for kids to use.

It's right now got a small saving of $20 at Amazon.

This is the one I'm yet to try, but I'm so excited by the idea. #173131. ‘Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element’: Yuko Mohri on her exhibition of found objects at London's Barbican

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1262 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

‘Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element’: Yuko Mohri on her exhibition of found objects at London's Barbican

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional highlights from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.
  • Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London.
  • The Art Newspaper: How did your Barb­ican residency come about?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional highlights from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.

Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London. At the show’s core is a series of site-responsive kinetic and sound installations made with objects she found at the Barbican. These objects, either stored away or nearly tossed out, embed the history and memories of this famed cultural centre, which will be closed for a year from June 2028 for a £191m revamp ahead of its 50th anniversary in 2032. According to Mohri, the pieces represent an ongoing process that may lead to imperfection, which she finds more profound than a picture-perfect scenario.

The Art Newspaper: How did your Barb­ican residency come about?

Yuko Mohri: When I was approached for a project at The Curve, I discussed with Inês Geraldes Cardoso, the curator of this exhibition, the possibility of researching the Barbican Centre.

Industry observers note that the Curve is a unique and challenging space, and they accept experimental projects with artists. I am not the kind of artist who needs to work within a white cube. I understand why they chose me to create something unique. I am, however, the kind of artist who needs time to understand the environment and identify interesting elements that already exist in that context. A research residency is necessary.

But rather than focusing on just this curved gallery space, I wanted to see what the Barbican really is. It is a huge centre involving many different departments and activities. Thousands of people are also living here in the attached residential complex.

After rounds of negotiations, I was offered a two-week residency to look for objects and meet the people living and working here. I got a temporary studio at The Pit, a small theatre space located in the basement.

Industry observers note that “Imperfection is everywhere,” Yuko Mohri says. “It’s a great element.” Photo: © Toby Coulson/Barbican Centre.

What were your biggest discoveries?

Recent findings suggest that the centre has many departments, but they seem very separate from each other and don’t have a lot of communication between them. But since they are going to have a major renovation, they want to revamp the centre’s system, too, and strengthen communication.

According to recent reports, we started researching different departments and looked for objects across all the spaces. I wanted to collect objects from here that resonate with the space.

Industry observers note that among the most iconic ones are the original Barbican lamps featured throughout this exhibition. These were once used as street lamps surrounding the centre and also in the building. But as time went on, they were replaced with those of a latest design. They were dusty and strange, but I immediately knew that I wanted to use them for my installation. So I spent a lot of time washing these lamps in my temporary studio.

Industry observers note that the speakers that I use for the latest iteration of the ongoing Decomposition series (begun 2021) located near the entrance to The Curve are old speakers from the Barbican. The found cables that I use to connect the fruit with the lamps and the sound are also very important to me. I also found these metal junk pieces that were discarded in a workshop, and I reappropriated them as triggers for the lamps in the installations in the middle part of the exhibition.

Throughout this project I met many people outside the gallery space, from engineers to the caretakers of the parking space. The extensive communication helped me connect with a lot of open-minded people who accept me and my work.

Yuko Mohri’s Moré Moré (Leaky) is an ongoing installation inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE.

How do you relate the centre’s characteristics with your practice?

The Barbican has many water leaks. There’s also a leak of sound because The Curve wraps around the concert hall. So these leaky elements resonate with my practice, especially my ongoing Moré Moré (Leaky) series (begun 2017), which was inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations and how the staff contain these water leaks with temporary fixes using everyday items. I presented a version of this in Venice.

This time at the Barbican, I created a large-scale installation located towards the exit of The Curve, using found objects such as a pot, an umbrella, plastic bottles, Wellington boots, traffic cones and old water sinks designed for the Barbican apartments.

I also keep the space open and transparent by removing the covers on the entrances and the back so that people can see what’s going on there from the outside. I also exposed the inner layers of the walls to give people a peek into what is behind them.

Are you building an ecosystem within the Barbican that makes the inaudible heard and the invisible seen?

In a recent development, instead of building, I see it as repairing. Inspired by attending concert rehearsals at the Barbican, I chose the title In Concert, which mirrors the Latin root consertare. It carries the meaning of repair and adjustment, resembling the process of making an organisation.

The process is also similar to making an installation. When I started, I had no idea how it would turn out eventually. I constantly make adjustments to the elements of my installations, like a conductor making adjustments to the tempo or the volume of the musical instruments. The title also reflects that what you see is not stable. Water leaks, gravity and the audience’s presence will change even some very tiny elements. It is not a finalised show. It’s an ongoing process.

Would you say that you are in control and at the same time you also let go?

I am a human being and I have a desire for a certain outcome. But somehow, it doesn’t always work. This trial and error process is a very learnable process for me.

Sources indicate that we all have our expectations, but our society and environment have become increasingly unstable. For example, this summer Tokyo rained non-stop for a record 36 consecutive days. We need to adjust our lives. It’s also a necessity when we are based in Tokyo, constantly facing natural disasters like earthquakes. Japan has long been isolated, but now we have many immigrants. Our society is changing. I see this as a kind of training and accept these changing forces. It’s not necessarily about making things perfect. Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element.

An edition of Mohri’s ongoing installation Decomposition from 2022 in Kanazawa, Japan Photo: Yuu Takagi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE.

Education: 2004 BFA, Tama Art University; 2006 MFA, Tokyo University of the Arts.

Key highlights: 2026 The Bass, Miami Beach; 2026 Yokohama Museum of Art; 2026 Centro Botín, Santander; 2025 Pirelli HangarBicocca, Milan; 2024 Japan Pavilion, Venice Biennale; 2023 14th Gwangju Biennale.

Represented by: Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York; Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tokyo; Mother’s Tankstation, London; White Space, Beijing; Project Fulfill Art Space, Taipei.

• Yuko Mohri: In Concert, Barbican Centre, London, until 24 January 2027.

Speaking to Itâs Nice That, Abbott points to cut-and-paste Whole Earth catalogues and 1970s Hallmark calendars, turning to historic open-source engravings and 40 typefaces pulled largely from free sites like DaFont and 1001 Fonts. âA good designer can make a free font look expensive,â he says. Inside, canary-yellow New York Native Seeds pages pair dried pods with numbered captions, while Letter from the Editor opens on a giant hot-pink drop-cap T.

Abrupt scale and color shifts keep the book moving without a single commissioned shoot. On George Musserâs Free Will, Inside and Out spread, slate-blue display letters stack behind a black ink spiral on warm yellow stock, opposite a tall block drop cap. The March calendar turns sideways, running massive dark serif letters up the left edge beside a blue sunrise-and-moonset grid. That same nerve drives Abbottâs editorial design for Mutt Art Review with founder Kara Kazanoff. They picked familiar, cheaper-to-license 1970s ITC fonts and pushed them hard. On Concerns Two, Three, and Four, translucent red, amber, and hot-pink titles overprint straight across black-and-white drawings and halftone boots so the art bleeds through. Glitch Five drops cover imagery altogether, letting white script and serif type hold a grey cover alone.

Inside Mutt Art Review, the font roster doesnât change, yet every essay gets a newly introduced grid. On Ted Joansâ Take on Liberty, matte black paper frames stepped white display type whose opening line curves directly into the text column opposite Joansâs torn 1962 sketchbook cover. On David Joselit and Janine Iversenâs interview, one sweeping ampersand fills half the left page. After seven years in-house at Dazed, Pitchfork, and Pioneer Works, Abbott went solo for print he can hold â publications whose press checks donât fit beside a day job. His advice for anyone chasing editorial design stays blunt: acquire books, test-print body copy sizes, learn rich versus process black, and donât get too precious.

#173128. Breaking: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2095 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll.
  • In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting owners’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

In a recent development, some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

In a recent development, on top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He indicates this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

It has been revealed that on top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

“We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”.

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

Recent findings suggest that “During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu indicates. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

It has been revealed that in general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu indicates. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, states Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.).

According to recent reports, at the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu states losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she states. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

Industry observers note that that means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he notes. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.).

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, notes Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Industry observers note that finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, states board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

Industry observers note that A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist owners stated the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”.

According to recent reports, for those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon indicates. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

Sources indicate that “Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”.

Sources indicate that desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer claims. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Recent findings suggest that sexual health, Dr. Dovec notes, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Sources indicate that not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”.

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The organization describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” remarked Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the company equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The manufacturer’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.
