Estudio A-G uses colour to revision 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.
  • Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
  • Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

It has been revealed that monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for fresh inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely upcoming, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”.

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing latest energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”.

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez noted, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

According to recent reports, the studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its latest owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez noted, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”.

In a recent development, he also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

Interior design: Estudio A-GFeatured furniture & design brands: Estudio A-G, Los Patrones, Herman Miller, Adhoc, Bibi Bibi, Comité de Proyectos, Alan SaenzFeatured artists: Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman, Adriana Silva.

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Mason & Fifth's Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact”

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Latest-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.
  • Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.
  • The tech giant has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Latest-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The tech giant has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

According to recent reports, just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Industry observers note that holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” noted the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

#173107. 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better.
  • It has been revealed that supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise.
  • It has been revealed that still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

It has been revealed that supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

It has been revealed that still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

According to recent reports, how it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular issues (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article remarked they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

What to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he claims.

In a recent development, what it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

In a recent development, who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack claims. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

How it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Sources indicate that why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of Newly introduced York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

It has been revealed that what to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, says Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

Recent findings suggest that how it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are important for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, notes. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

In a recent development, what to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

How it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov claims. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research shows iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

It has been revealed that what to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

How it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

Recent findings suggest that why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple concerns for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan notes. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

In a recent development, what to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

“When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati claims. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

#173106. Argentina leads the way in repatriating Indigenous human remains, study indicates

Argentina leads the way in repatriating Indigenous human remains, study indicates

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display.
  • It has been revealed that “Argentina is central to any discussion of this problem in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper.
  • Recent findings suggest that the researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display. A recent study by the Chilean researchers Jacinta Arthur and Patricia Ayala suggests that the movement has opened a crucial ethical debate in both countries, with key differences: while Chile has handled repatriation campaigns on a case-by-case basis, Argentina has emerged as a regional leader since passing a law specifically tackling the issue.

It has been revealed that “Argentina is central to any discussion of this problem in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper. “In Chile, by contrast, there is no legal framework of this kind. That is why it was both necessary and interesting to compare the two realities.”.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity. It emerged from Arthur and Ayala’s work with Indigenous communities in Chile, particularly the campaigns led by the Atacameño and Rapa Nui people, where demands for the respectful treatment of human remains include critiques of their scientific study, museum display, sample collection, repatriation and reburial.

It has been revealed that those efforts were underscored last July, when the Australian Museum in Sydney returned the remains of ancestors of the Rapa Nui people who had been removed from sacred burial sites at Rano Raraku during a German naval expedition in 1882, and acquired by the museum the following year. The institution’s director, Kim McKay, publicly acknowledged the circumstances under which the ancestors’ remains had entered the collection, and remarked: “Returning them is an act of moral responsibility.”.

According to Ayala, despite the legal differences between Argentina and Chile, the treatment of human remains from an Indigenous perspective “has not yet become central to scientific concerns”. Indigenous activism, she claims, has forced museums and archaeologists to confront “the exclusion of Indigenous voices” and “alternative knowledge and ontologies” linked to ancestral bodies and the materials associated with them. It has also brought renewed attention to the violence of looting, collecting and scientific research that helped shape colonial and national museums, where Indigenous ancestral remains have ended up since at least the 19th century.

“In this context, both museums and academic fields have begun to reflect on their practices and discourses,” Ayala claims, “although much work remains to be done to fully integrate the rights of Indigenous peoples in both countries.”.

Argentina passed a law in 2001 mandating that Indigenous human remains held in public or private collections must be made available to the peoples or communities that claim them. An implementing decree followed in 2010, making the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs responsible for surveying and identifying remains, and coordinating their return.

Sources indicate that A recent case at the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti, part of the Universidad de Buenos Aires, indicates how such restitutions unfold in practice. Last May the museum returned the remains of an Inca child from Apu Chañi, along with his grave goods, to El Angosto and Sol de Mayo, two communities in the El Moreno area of Jujuy state. The child had entered the museum’s collection in 1905, after being brought down from a hill on Nevado de Chañi. Following the restitution, a mausoleum was built at the foot of the mountain to display the grave goods, while the child’s remains will be buried at high altitude when conditions in the freezing high Andes allow.

“What I think is missing here, above all, is getting ahead of restitutions, not waiting for communities to file a claim,” Andrea Pegoraro, the director of the Museo Etnográfico, tells The Art Newspaper. Pegoraro, notes the return of the child from Apu Chañi indicates that Argentina has a more developed legal framework than many neighbouring countries, but also exposes the limits of a policy based solely on responding to claims.

That, she notes, is one of the challenges still facing Argentine museums: moving from responding to specific requests to actively reviewing collections, identifying provenance gaps, reconstructing acquisition histories and contacting the relevant communities. In the Apu Chañi case, she says, the museum reviewed archival and archaeological records to establish where the remains had been taken and to which community they should be returned.

At the restitution ceremony, Pegoraro said the museum was not handing over “a heritage object or an object of study”, but rather “an ancestor to his territory and his people”. The community, in turn, described the returned ancestor as “a guardian” connected to water and life in the Puna region of Jujuy.

According to recent reports, for Pegoraro, the distinction between human remains and objects is crucial. “If they are human remains, I am fully in favour of returning them, and the community must decide what to do with them,” she states. Objects raise a different set of considerations, in her view: to whom they should be returned, what happens to them and how museums can ensure access for other communities.

Industry observers note that reconstructing provenance is essential to any restitution process, Pegoraro adds, because Indigenous territories do not always align with today’s political boundaries. “Communities inhabit territories that did not previously have the political or geographical boundaries we have today,” she says. Museums often rely on documentation archaeologists wrote at the time the remains entered a collection, even when the places they recorded no longer correspond neatly to current jurisdictions.

Recent findings suggest that pegoraro also warns that change cannot be limited to isolated restitutions. “The integration of Indigenous communities does not come only through rhetoric, or by carrying out a restitution or holding an exhibition once in a while, but by literally working side by side,” she notes. She adds that collaboration must include the ongoing rewriting of exhibition narratives, as well as financial compensation.

Recent findings suggest that in Pegoraro’s view, the current movement for repatriation of Indigenous remains and artefacts began in the 1980s, especially in the US, Australia, Upcoming Zealand and Canada. In Argentina and elsewhere in South America, she adds, those demands gained force with the return of democracy after dictatorships. In Europe, however, museums carry “a much stronger colonial history”, she notes, and while some countries are beginning to talk about decolonising collections, returning objects or rewriting narratives, “they still have a long way to go. It must not remain just rhetoric.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that denver Design District has unveiled a slick newly introduced brand identity, transforming the once exclusive design commerce hub into a fresh cultural destination. A blend of design-focused goods, art, retail and food, the new identity marks a more accessible, culturally relevant district made for the masses.

While there's no formula for creating the best rebrands, Denver Design District's upcoming identity shines in its attention to detail, honouring its rich design heritage while embracing a newfound playfulness. Sleek, timeless and characterful, the new brand identity is the ultimate love letter to design.

Sources indicate that created in collaboration with D4 Urban and design studio Wunder Werkz, the Denver Design District rebrand centres around a wonderfully contemporary brandmark. Representing the district's evolution, the 3 'Ds' motif compresses the bold letterforms by a third each time, making for a dynamic visual anchor.

To accomodate the brandmark, Wunder Werkz created DDD Standard, a bespoke midweight sans serif, to act as the district's display typeface. Equal parts "architectural and playful", it draws inspiration from Herbert Bayer's mid-century furniture forms. Paired with an iconographic system of silhouetted design products, clarity and cohesion flow throughout the identity with a confident authority.

It has been revealed that “The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, Partner at Wunder Werkz. “Trade remains an key part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”.

Recent findings suggest that A rich colour system of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow contrasts the tans and greys of the district's buildings, bringing warmth and personality to the clean design. The result is a refined homage to design that feels accessible and unpretentious, without losing the slick essence of the design district.

It has been revealed that “This project represents the kind of work we love most because it allows us to engage at every level, from strategy and stakeholder alignment through implementation and installation,” adds Hartman. “For us, that’s where the best work happens. Not when design is treated as an afterthought, but when it becomes the link between strategy, space and experience. The result is a brand that feels cohesive at every scale, from a website headline to a warehouse-sized building facade.”.

“Denver Design District has always been rooted in great design, but our vision for its future is much broader,” states Dan Cohen, CEO of Denver Design District. “This rebrand isn’t about changing who we are, it’s about reflecting what the District is becoming: a more dynamic, connected, and welcoming destination for Denver and the entire Rocky Mountain region.”.

#173104. Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

📅 13 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1511 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that at some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married?
  • For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office.
  • It has been revealed that joan listed a few traits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she says, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

It has been revealed that joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

Recent findings suggest that “No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”.

According to recent reports, it landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

It has been revealed that for much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

Recent findings suggest that you can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of users on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift indicates up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

But perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”.

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

As Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Blueprint B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

According to recent reports, “I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”.

Sources indicate that the practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo indicates. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

Of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

It has been revealed that “Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh says. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

Alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”.

Industry observers note that in 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a newly introduced career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

In a recent development, “I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

It has been revealed that rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

According to recent reports, recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

But that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

It takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.

Ragged Edge gives US fintech Tilt a brand identity built on trust: a signature logo, tilted script type and chartreuse grit.

Industry observers note that the idea lands in the first frame. A signature-style Tilt logo, handwritten and leaning, sits against stark black and white, with chartreuse doing all the shouting. Heavy grotesque headlines carry the lines, Credit for what you're capable of and Tilt the odds in your favor, and one italic script word inside each line does the leaning: capable, favor, all. Under the headline, six portraits run in a row, each captioned with a first name and the words good for it. The promise belongs to the people in the pictures. Black and white say no nonsense. Chartreuse claims urgency.

According to recent reports, the type system is two voices in one grid. The grotesque runs huge and tight, stacked in short lines that fill the poster edge to edge, while the custom script tilts inside it, one italic word per line doing the emphasis. On the manifesto poster the same pairing slows down: Imagine a world where simply trying tallies up sits above a short paragraph in small, even type, ending on the line Because we know you're good for it. The app screens keep the discipline. The script logo rides at the top of black screens, the grotesque handles the numbers, $400 for a Cash Advance, $50 and $25 for a savings target, and the chartreuse button is the only color allowed to shout.

In a recent development, the system holds at every scale. A desert billboard reads Credit history is in the past in black on white, a subway poster claims Value is already in you, a taxi top carries You're capable. We're credit. The same lines shrink onto a chartreuse notebook, a Tilt Visa card in a tray of keys and coins, and a yellow desk mug that reads Working on it. Pearl Chuaynarong's brushstroke illustrations run through the product screens, a food stall steaming, a wallet spilling cards, loose and painterly against the strict grid, keeping the mess of real effort inside the system instead of cleaning it out.

Latest Update: 5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship.
  • In a recent development, most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going.
  • You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

In a recent development, most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

In a recent development, to be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

It has been revealed that “At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

According to recent reports, venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That mentioned, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

It has been revealed that if someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher states. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

It has been revealed that maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” plans fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

It has been revealed that “In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher says, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds states. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how important it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your big day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely reveals empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

According to recent reports, ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That noted, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”.

Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee.

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

Industry observers note that the one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock.

It has been revealed that once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Recent findings suggest that hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

What makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. It has been revealed that for 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Industry observers note that hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. #173096. After nearly two decades, the Old Acropolis Museum in Athens re-opens

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (848 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

After nearly two decades, the Old Acropolis Museum in Athens re-opens

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Old Acropolis Museum, the first Greek museum to be built in modern times, re-opened on Monday after a major restoration project.
  • The opening ceremony was a grand affair, with speeches by the Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and the country’s minister of culture Lina Mendoni, among others.
  • It has been revealed that once simply the “Museum”, the Old Acropolis Museum took its current name in 2009, when Athens built a newer Acropolis Museum 300 yards down the hill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Old Acropolis Museum, the first Greek museum to be built in modern times, re-opened on Monday after a major restoration project. It is the first time the museum, founded in 1874 and nestled into the rock of the storied Acropolis hill, has been accessible to the public since 2007.

The opening ceremony was a grand affair, with speeches by the Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and the country’s minister of culture Lina Mendoni, among others.

It has been revealed that once simply the “Museum”, the Old Acropolis Museum took its current name in 2009, when Athens built a newer Acropolis Museum 300 yards down the hill. This offered larger and state-of-the-art space in which to house the antiquities from the Parthenon and other Greek sites, as well as a viewing room designed for the Elgin Marbles—presently showing casts, but with the idea that one day the museum might one day welcome the real items.

Industry observers note that the Old Acropolis Museum was left empty for years, and intends eventually developed to use it as storage and administrative spaces. But by 2019, the Greek state definitively nixed this idea.

Industry observers note that “For us, it was inconceivable, almost an affront, that this historic building, with its unique location, should be converted into offices and storage facilities,” said Mendoni during her opening speech. “We therefore decided that the museum should reopen in accordance with its original purpose. However, it was not to become just another conventional museum, but rather a museum and exhibition space hosting exhibitions on the history, archaeology and culture of Athens, as well as contemporary art exhibitions inspired by Greek civilisation and innovative programmes incorporating cutting-edge technology.”.

Recent findings suggest that the museum will now host both a rotating selection of artefacts as well as a contemporary art programme. The first exhibition, Athens City Idea, focuses on Athens as a social, political, and economic entity, via tragic masks, statues, coins, and amphorae that have been in storage elsewhere across Athens, plus recent discoveries. A digital art component animated the Parthenon’s friezes and the history of the Acropolis Hill.

Part of the idea behind the temporary exhibitions is to keep the museum’s display current, a point also underlined by its commitment to contemporary art.

This includes the last of a trilogy of works commissioned for Athens from the American artist Michael Rakowitz, which is also the final project of Neon, the roving art foundation created by Dimitris Daskalopoulos that for 14 years has funded art and exhibitions across the city, and which declared its closure earlier this year.

Industry observers note that “You could say that the first contemporary work here was Phidias’s statue of Athena in the 5th century BCE,” quipped Daskalopoulos, the Athens-born collector who founded Neon. Daskalopoulos also supported the refurbishment of the Old Acropolis Museum, which was funded by both private and public money. “But encouraging the coexistence of antiquity with the contemporary is a challenge we have embraced many times throughout our work at Neon.”.

Michael Rakowitz and Elina Kountouri, the director of Neon, outside the reopened Old Acropolis Museum.

Rakowitz’s installation What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026), which was commissioned by Neon, and comprises a kiln and newly fired bricks, looks at a lesser-known episode in the Acropolis’s history.

“I realised that you could only tell the whole story of the site if you look through the lens of migration,” the artist told The Art Newspaper. He studied the population exchanges during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, when Greece and Turkey forced a combined total of around 1.5 million inhabitants to leave—Christian Turks to Greece and Muslim Greeks to Turkey. When the Turkish refugees arrived in Athens, they set up tents and encampments at the base of the Acropolis hill.

Industry observers note that “Thinking about a ruin as being something that can renew itself to a population and become once again a shelter excited me,” he remarked. "When I found out about the tradition of the Asia Minor refugees who were able to go back to Turkey after some years, and then the Muslims who were uprooted from Greece, when those populations were able to visit their the departed homelands, they found oftentimes their buildings or towns in a state of ruin, and they would take a brick from that place and bring it back as a memento.”.

Installation view of Michael Rakowitz, What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026).

Industry observers note that courtesy the artist and Neon. Commissioned by Neon. © Natalia Tsoukala.

Recent findings suggest that rakowitz has incorporated these original bricks alongside ones newly made with inscriptions and stamps that bear witness to more recent histories of displacement. For these he worked with survivors of the 1920s population transfers as well as women in the Melissa Network, a nonprofit organisation that supports migrant women in Greece.

“I wanted these bricks to become a foundation for a latest kind of city that welcomes strangers and doesn't push them back at sea,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.
  • The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.
  • Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by José Hevia.

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.

Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for latest solutions to add more light.

“Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight,” studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a “modern translation of the old wells” that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house’s upper level.

The 40-square-metre lower level houses an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area, a bathroom and a small study.

This can be partitioned off from the living space using folding doors made from wood and rice paper, inspired by the clients’ time living in Japan.

In the kitchen, Sánchez stated he added a mirror-clad island to “introduce a sense of fragility without disrupting the open feel of the space”.

The upper level, meanwhile, houses the home’s bedrooms and a bathroom. The two floors are connected by the Klein-blue lightwell, which has oculi on all four sides to help distribute the illumination from its skylight throughout the space.

Sánchez wanted to “bring that picturesque atmosphere of Aiguafreda Street into the house, making it part of its surroundings by reclaiming that well – now translated into a lightwell that also helps regulate the home’s temperature.”.

This was one of many tailor-made solutions to turn the former laundry house into a home.

“There were many challenges, both technical – access to the mezzanine level, the new staircase, the structural reinforcements – and functional, like fitting the program into just 80 square metres,” Sánchez noted.

His studio also worked with materials that would complement the existing ones, using terracotta tiles on the ground floor to extend the traditional exterior clay paving and adding colored glazed tiles to the washbasins and bathroom walls.

“Ultimately, the goal is always to create a cohesive, overarching project that addresses all these challenges and offers something extra – something almost hard to put into words, but that translates into simply feeling good in the space,” Sánchez concluded.

Rául Sánchez Architects is currently working on the final phase of the project, the design of its orchard and garden, which will begin at the start of 2027.

The studio also recently designed a concrete home with a sunken courtyard in Cala Tamarit.

Architecture team: Nerea Moya, Marta Gámiz, FlaviaStructure consultant: Diagonal EstructurasEngineering consultant: Mares Engyniers.

London Museum brings "back a bit of London's heritage" with Smithfield Market opening

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.
  • Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.
  • According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Hufton + Crow.

Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.

According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum’s relocation from the Barbican Estate’s former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market, which is expected to open in 2028.

“There’s an opportunity to represent London as it is now and in the future, and really take city museums to another level,” stated London Museum’s New Museum Project director Alec Shaw.

“We’re bringing back a bit of London’s heritage – one building that has not been seen or encountered for at least 30 years, and the other one an amazing architectural gem that hasn’t been fully appreciated and will now be,” he told Dezeen.

The main entrance to the London Museum is marked by a covered street, West Poultry Avenue, which doubles as the Real Time gallery that stretches between the General Market and Poultry Market.

Entering the transformed Victorian market, visitors pass a museum shop and an auditorium before entering Our Time – an expansive gallery illuminated from above by an oculus.

Shops that once wrapped the perimeter of the market trading floor were removed to open up the space, but the restoration was designed to retain hints of the building fabric’s history.

“You can see pockets in the brickwork walls where joists of the first floor and little plaster columns were originally located,” said Julian Harrap Architects partner Lyall Thow.

“There was a second floor, represented by a darkened band where we didn’t overly clean the brickwork, and fireplaces in the upper offices were taken out, restored, and put back where they would have been originally.”.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects overhauled 42 individual shops that formerly encircled the General Market into 12 multi-storey units.

Six units were kept to contain a restaurant, galleries and learning spaces, while the other six were left for the museum to invite partner institutions to occupy.

“What the ‘museum of tomorrow’ will be is not just a single institute, but a coral reef of small institutes that can plug in – Dezeen could have an office here, a leather upholsterer might have a craft workshop here, restaurants and pop-ups…” said Khan.

“This living ecosystem, which is reflective of the city, is possible because of this market building we’ve moved into,” he continued.

Recent findings suggest that “What we’ve done is make openings, windows, and cuts through the floor and ceiling, which allow that energy to emanate out of the city and for the city’s energy to emanate inwards,” added Khan. “At the centre of it all is this enormous public space, the General Market ground floor, where anything can happen.”.

A staircase takes visitors down to London’s Roman street level, to the museum’s permanent Past Time exhibition, which displays precious artefacts.

The restored brickwork walls in the subterranean space are interrupted by a six-metre window, revealing passing Thameslink trains.

A series of underground vaults that were discovered during the museum’s construction will open to visitors in spring 2027.

“This museum epitomises the idea of the primordial reflex in us to dig to find various treasures,” said Stanton Williams co-founder Paul Williams.

The architects aimed to make the qualities of the existing spaces work to the museum’s advantage, displaying delicate objects in the underground gallery and maintaining the communal feel of the market space on ground level.

“Decisions based on the building – like precious objects should be kept underground because it’s got a greater thermal inertia – loosen the straitjacket around the museum having to act like a museum in other spaces,” noted Khan.

“It means some other spaces can be more market-like and have a more public-facing potential that a normal museum wouldn’t be able to do,” he continued. “The building has enabled the museum to become a different kind of museum.”.

Unisex toilets were designed in a Victorian style, with decorative tiles depicting wildflowers that grew in London’s bombed-out sites.

Elsewhere in the museum is a 24-hour cafe where original interior tiles and a timber staircase were restored.

Shaw hopes the London Museum will be an inviting place that residents and tourists want to return to time and again.

Recent findings suggest that “We want to be super welcoming – we don’t want to be intimidating as a museum,” stated Shaw. “Some of the other museums are quite imposing buildings.”.

“We want to be a destination, not just a museum, but a place for people to keep coming back to.”.

Other museums recently completed in London include V&A East by O’Donnell + Tuomey and the V&A East Storehouse by Diller Scofidio + Renfro, which was given a Dezeen Award for its wayfinding design.

Photography by Hufton + Crow.

Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that barefoot walks on the beach.
  • Sources indicate that using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not fresh, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • Recent findings suggest that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—massive and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Sources indicate that using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not fresh, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Recent findings suggest that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

Sources indicate that “It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” says Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

In a recent development, patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting newly introduced collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” notes Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

According to recent reports, this type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” says Dr. Pearl.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

In a recent development, try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

In a recent development, for cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

Recent findings suggest that but will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” says Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

Industry observers note that if you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

If injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a blueprint to minimize your pain.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1121 w)
