In a recent development, wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

It has been revealed that aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

According to recent reports, baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Industry observers note that did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar complications).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Sources indicate that another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Sources indicate that witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

In a recent development, blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

According to recent reports, some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

In a recent development, using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

It has been revealed that ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That remarked, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

Wine bar informs rich colour palette for Yorkshire home renovation by Tuckey Design Studio

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Fran Mart.

London architecture practice Tuckey Design Studio has renovated and extended Bay House in rural Yorkshire, using a rich, moody palette intended to evoke the feeling of a wine bar.

The project involved reconfiguring and expanding the country house dating from the early 2000s, while introducing a garden spa and sauna.

Tuckey Design Studio was tasked by the clients to recreate the feeling of their favourite wine bar, which informed a palette of dark timber carpentry, terracotta-painted walls and a bespoke wine storage cabinet alongside a tasting area.

“The ambition was clear from the beginning: to bring the atmosphere of a much-loved London wine bar into the home,” project lead Fraser Biggins told Dezeen.

“The clients’ enthusiasm for wine and music became important touchstones for the design, informing both the arrangement of the spaces and the character of the interiors,” he added.

The home’s previously cramped interiors are now centred on a large, double-height atrium, which serves as both a point of arrival and a gathering and tasting space with a bespoke timber “wine wall”.

This hall is finished with dark timber panelling, terrazzo floors and terracotta paintwork, with a wall alongside an arched composite stone staircase punctured by small square openings.

This central space leads through into the social spaces, with a kitchen and dining space finished using similar dark timber panelling and concrete countertops.

Industry observers note that the stairs lead up to the first floor via a landing with a built-in bench, where a balcony connecting the bedrooms enjoys views of the hall below. It also looks across the garden through windows in a new bay window extension.

“The central hall forms the organising principle of the house, providing a shared space from which the surrounding family rooms and activities unfold,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“A series of interconnected spaces, galleries and overlooking balconies create visual connections across different levels, allowing the house to feel both connected and varied,” he added.

On the first floor, two of the existing bedrooms have been converted into a games room and bar space, finished in dark shades of green and grey.

Alongside them are four ensuite bedrooms finished in warmer shades of pale pink and yellow, with each featuring a hand-painted mural designed to “reflect the character of each occupant”.

“Material choices were guided by a desire for honesty, durability and longevity,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“We wanted the spaces to feel timeless and comfortable, without relying too heavily on traditional materials or references.”.

“Instead, the palette brings together robust, tactile finishes that feel natural and lived-in, allowing the character of the materials to speak for themselves,” he added.

The exterior of the extension has been finished in composite stone and dark accoya wood, and looks across the home’s garden to the standalone spa and sauna, which was designed as a “complementary counterpoint” to the main home.

Previous projects by Tuckey Design Studio include a home in Wiltshire constructed using walls of unstabilised rammed earth and a residence within a converted chapel in Devon.

Photography by Fran Mart.

#173019. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1700 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

It has been revealed that sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

Sources indicate that all things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

In a recent development, regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin claims. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, indicates Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin claims. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin indicates. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

That’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, notes Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

It has been revealed that over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra notes, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

It has been revealed that because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition complications and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar claims. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research reveals that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that as researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s key to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A large light well brings daylight deep into this private home that was designed by Desai Chia Architecture for a tight site in a dense Maryland neighbourhood.
  • The project takes its name from its location in Bethesda, a city located northwest of Washington DC.
  • The house is set within a suburban neighbourhood near the downtown district, where residential lots are about one-fifth of an acre (647 square metres).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jake Balston.

A large light well brings daylight deep into this private home that was designed by Desai Chia Architecture for a tight site in a dense Maryland neighbourhood.

The project takes its name from its location in Bethesda, a city located northwest of Washington DC.

The house is set within a suburban neighbourhood near the downtown district, where residential lots are about one-fifth of an acre (647 square metres). Because the houses here are close together, the architects needed to be very mindful of privacy concerns.

“The clients sought a house that would feel open and light-filled without sacrificing privacy,” said New York-based Desai Chia Architecture.

“Its compact lot and the close proximity of neighbouring houses required a careful response balancing both openness and discretion.”.

The architects intended the house to “rethink suburban-urban hybrid living through a modern lens”.

Roughly rectangular in strategy, it has three levels and a basement. Setbacks help break up the mass, particularly on the street-facing elevation.

The building appears “as a two-storey building from several vantage points,” the team mentioned.

“The home is carefully scaled to blend with neighbouring houses, balancing a strong architectural identity with sensitivity to its suburban context,” the team stated.

In a recent development, facades are clad in grey fibre-cement panels made to last for a century. The material is known for protecting against fire, pests and extreme weather, according to the team.

“A durable, low-maintenance exterior with a strong architectural presence was a key client priority from the outset,” the architects stated.

“Glass-fibre-reinforced concrete (GRFC) panels were selected to create a crisp, sculptural facade that captures texture and shifting light throughout the day.”.

A modern-style bay window adds dimension and visual interest to the front and back facades.

Within the home, public spaces are located on the ground level. The rear portion opens into a yard with a lap pool.

The upper levels contain bedrooms and two offices, and the top floor has a rooftop terrace. The basement holds a gym, ping-pong area and media room.

A limited number of windows helps ensure privacy. To provide natural illumination, the team created a three-storey light well, which is positioned along a central staircase and brings daylight deep into the dwelling.

“This vertical, faceted volume allows sunlight to cascade downward, distributing diffuse light from a small skylight across circulation spaces on multiple levels while minimising solar heat gain,” Desai Chia Architecture remarked.

Sources indicate that the all-electric house has a geothermal heating and cooling system. To enable the homeowners to age in place, the house has a shaft where an ADA-compliant elevator could be added in the future.

The homeowners are physicians, one of whom can walk to his practice in downtown Bethesda.

“When needed, the dedicated home offices allow both physicians to work from home in spaces with calming natural light,” the studio said.

“Its location – easily walkable to downtown amenities and robust public transit – supports a connected pattern of work and family life.”.

Other homes in Maryland include a restored carriage house by Colleen Healey Architecture that features colourful facade panels and a family home by Ziger Snead clad in stone shingles, charred wood and weathering steel.

Design architect: Desai Chia ArchitectureArchitect of record: Thomson & Cooke Architects.

Photography by Jake Balston.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food.

That being remarked, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

Recent findings suggest that L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:.

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:.

Recent findings suggest that L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

Industry observers note that however, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.).

According to recent reports, and though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.).

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being stated, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:.

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives “more time for their craft”.
  • Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the upgrade spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.
  • Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives “more time for their craft”.

Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the upgrade spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.

Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly – its AI creative studio – through the Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta.

Consumers can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.

The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity.

Adobe has also rolled out Firefly Design in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.

Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.

Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.

Adobe remarked the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being asked to turn projects around faster.

The brand’s latest approach aims to tackle this by bringing “AI assistance and collaboration directly into the Adobe tools they rely on”.

Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud at Adobe, mentioned the aim is to protect what makes a creative’s work distinctive.

“The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out,” mentioned Subramaniam.

“Our latest Creative Cloud innovations transform our trusted creative tools into agentic, intelligent workflows that give pros the precision, control and flexibility to explore their ideas, streamline their work and stay focused on the creative decisions that make their work uniquely theirs.”.

Industry observers note that the Creative Agent – which Adobe describes as a creative partner – now powers AI Assistants (currently in beta) across Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io. In Photoshop, the assistant is available only in the Photoshop beta app.

The agent handles multi-step tasks behind the scenes, letting professionals delegate work and increase their creative velocity while remaining “in the director’s chair”.

In Premiere, the agent now supports new capabilities, including applying an effect to every clip in a sequence, tracking a masked subject through a frame, and adjusting colour and exposure across a whole sequence at once.

Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations, which allow external AI agents to connect with its software.

The integrations will let owners instruct third-party agents of their choice to work inside Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, editing project files directly on their own computer.

Industry observers note that layers, vectors and sequences stay fully editable throughout the process, so customers can “step in at any moment to refine the work by hand”. The local MCP integrations will be available in private beta in early 2027.

According to recent reports, if a user’s chosen third-party agent is also connected to other MCP-capable tools, such as Google Drive or Slack, it can bring them into the same workflow. For example, it could pull in a brief from Google Docs, work on the project using Adobe’s tools and share the result with colleagues in Slack.

Recent findings suggest that adobe has also added several updates that give Firefly users more say over how the AI assistant works. Creatives are now able to save their preferred formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products to be applied consistently in future projects.

According to recent reports, A newly introduced strategy mode lets owners review, edit and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, or leave the agent to run on its own. Adobe explained that creators remain in control, “guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve”.

Customers can also choose which AI model the agent works with, or let the agent select the best fit for the task.

In Firefly Boards, the agent can help develop mood boards, storyboards and concepts through conversation as they take shape in real time, “guided by human taste and direction”.

Adobe also introduced a preview of always-on agents to carry out routine jobs, such as sorting new files or preparing content for different platforms, “even when the customer steps away”.

Firefly’s video, design and image editors have also been updated, with the aim of taking projects from initial idea to finished work in a single workflow.

Among the other additions are a gallery of ready-made, quick actions, visual boards, and node-bases workflows through Firefly Graph (beta), which lets users build repeatable workflows of their own.

Adobe’s examples include turning a video storyboard into a finished cut and, in Firefly Design, carrying a brand identity from initial concept through client review within a single design workspace.

To learn more about the updates, visit Adobe’s website.

Industry observers note that inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Recent findings suggest that nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

In a recent development, nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Recent findings suggest that inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

According to recent reports, grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

It has been revealed that grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or concerns with breastfeeding.

It has been revealed that grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any challenges.

In a recent development, so, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:.

It has been revealed that sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

Sources indicate that for some fresh parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

It has been revealed that there are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:.

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:.

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

According to recent reports, it involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

Industry observers note that if they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Sources indicate that grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Recent findings suggest that yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Industry observers note that inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Industry observers note that often, they need no treatment. But if they cause complications or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The London maker of Milan design week’s much-discussed inflatable coffee table has unveiled his debut furniture collection, which includes veiny wax chairs and a rug adorned with cattle tags.
  • Jabez Bartlett is a British production-turned-furniture designer who caused a stir during April’s Milan design week, where he demonstrated a pillowy PVC coffee table topped with an opalescent resin surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by George Darrell unless stated otherwise.

The London maker of Milan design week’s much-discussed inflatable coffee table has unveiled his debut furniture collection, which includes veiny wax chairs and a rug adorned with cattle tags.

Jabez Bartlett is a British production-turned-furniture designer who caused a stir during April’s Milan design week, where he demonstrated a pillowy PVC coffee table topped with an opalescent resin surface.

A circular version followed, and both pieces are part of The Freight Proportioned to the Groove, an exhibition of his debut furniture collection that opens today in Hackney, London.

Bartlett told Dezeen that he wanted to start creating furniture to experiment with materials that he has used to bring film sets to life on screen.

Industry observers note that “With set design, things don’t necessarily have to be practical,” remarked the Devon-born designer. “It’s all about how they look on camera. I wanted to play with this in a more material and physical world.”.

“There’s a lot of industrial materials we’ve always used that I think are incredibly beautiful,” he continued. “It’s interesting to use something heavy and practical in a luxury piece.”.

Bartlett’s collection includes a triptych of marbled dining chairs made from a mixture of microcrystalline and crude oil wax cast in plywood frames.

The pieces were informed by a Japanese games table owned by the designer, characterised by a gridded top.

“I had the idea to remake it as a giant candle, with a wick in each square,” he explained. The idea became three chunky chairs that resemble large candles, embellished with playful wicks.

Bartlett’s collection also features a trio of lighting pieces clad in stretchy latex skins.

The smallest is a ceramic table lamp with a bloated shade, while the other two are angular floor lamps supported by metal structures, one of which was on display at the southwest London gallery Saatchi Yates earlier this year.

Despite their industrial materials, Bartlett also considers his pieces as nods to the wilderness.

It has been revealed that “I started off wanting to make brutalist-folk furniture, and now I’m seeing it, I feel like I got there,” he noted. “Memory and illusion play a significant part, and of course, growing up in Devon leaves an imprint of the natural and the ancient world on you.”.

Another of the collection’s pieces is a large diamond-patterned textile rug, overdyed and bleached, and embellished with metal tags normally used to identify cattle.

The tags hem the rug and were also embroidered into its fabric in decorative circles.

Also on display in the exhibition are a monolithic cast acrylic mirror, a glossy black plinth and column with protruding thorns and another floor lamp with a similarly spiky, elongated black body and a sandy leather shade.

The title of Bartlett’s exhibition refers to the final line of poet Emily Dickinson’s 19th-century poem, That Love is All There Is.

The Freight Proportioned to the Groove is on display from 26 to 29 November at Tuscany Wharf, 4B Orsman Road, London N1 5QJ. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

Photography by George Darrell unless stated otherwise.

Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

📅 31 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people.
  • According to recent reports, but do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne?
  • Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”.

According to recent reports, but do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Recent findings suggest that adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Industry observers note that salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

In a recent development, adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more swiftly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Recent findings suggest that which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Industry observers note that adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate newly introduced cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

According to recent reports, adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Recent findings suggest that though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Sources indicate that feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles-based artist Lucy McRae has created tactile, custom-made designs for sci-fi mini-series Blade Runner 2099 that veer away from the traditionally cold and metallic aesthetic of the films.

The show, which premiered on Wednesday on Amazon Prime, is the latest in the Blade Runner universe and follows Cora, a human fugitive played by actor Hunter Schafer.

She goes undercover as a replicant – a synthetic human – blade runner with veteran replicant Olwen, played by actor Michelle Yeoh, to track down a runaway carrying a secret that could destabilise the city.

McRae joined the production in 2022 as the official futurist of the show, after showrunner Silka Luisa saw her previous work exploring the relationship between emerging technology and human biology.

Her speculative work on body futurism later became direct visual references for the show and McRae was asked to speculate on human consciousness in 50 years’ time, with a specific focus on memory, bio-engineering, replicants’ sensuality, sex and family.

“I created a world-build of those questions, through scale models, building concepts through physical materials,” McRae told Dezeen. “These ideas begin to transpire within the show.”.

McRae designed the film’s birth bags, which are incubator-like sacks used to birth or transform replicants.

She also made the crèche set, the facility and replicant birth system that support the birth bags, as well as a skin polymer traction machine that was used for healing the protagonist Cora.

McRae also designed the material and colour palette for replicants, which includes pipes, quilting and industrial materials that fit the interiors of Olwen’s spacecraft and the padding around the traction machine.

The birth bag is a newly introduced iteration of McRae’s Compression Cradle, a project presented at the 2019 Milan Triennale exhibition Broken Nature.

It was a machine that offered a simulated hug to a person craving intimacy using an inflatable device.

In Blade Runner 2099, the design scale expanded dramatically, with nine vertical Compression Cradles created inside the Tyrell building where they functioned as birth bags in the show.

Sources indicate that mcRae often describes herself as a “body architect”. At Future Sensitive, the art-research lab she leads, her work revolves around using the body as a means to speculate on the future.

A few of her recent projects have explored what McRae calls the touch crisis – the idea that, with the rise of technology, digital devices might start to vie for human affection, and physical contact with other humans might suffer as a result.

Her Heavy Duty Love, for example, created for the Venice Architecture Biennale 2021, imagines a machine replacement of a parent’s embrace in a world where humans are grown in artificial wombs.

With The Future Day Spa, meanwhile, she presented a machine that could replace human contact altogether.

McRae’s states her focus on material tactility – such as creases, wrinkles, and squishy textures – adds a femininity to the show.

The series is built on the sci-fi intellectual property that followed from the original 1982 film and its aesthetic was historically labelled as metallic, cold, slick and masculine.

“The physicalisation of the work I do, the texture, achieves the femininity the show was after,” stated McRae. “It’s an absolute masterpiece where both violence and femininity coexist.”.

She also believes that by domesticating science and rendering technology malleable and wet, it creates a positive future that feels within human grasp and participation.

According to recent reports, “It feels positive because it feels within my grasp. I feel I can participate and I can contribute,” remarked McRae. “Whereas if it’s a future that doesn’t look or feel or belong to something that I understand, then it feels like it’s a closed door.”.

The designer said her work for the series, and in general, aims to focus on plausible futures rather than pure fantasy, while raising open-ended questions and encouraging audiences to navigate uncertainty with hope.

“What’s important for Silka and for my work is that anything I’m dealing with is never fantasy,” remarked McRae.

“I think physicalising possibility allows us to wear it, touch it and be able to get close to something that is far away but then allows us to see if it’s a fit, see if it belongs.”.

It has been revealed that “What I’m trying to do is create opportunities for people to ask these questions themselves and for me to not answer them. It’s going to be open-ended and unanswered because we don’t live in a world where one answer or many answers fit.”.

"How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.
  • The last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in Newly introduced York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught.
  • During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.

The last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in Newly introduced York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught. How had these young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?

During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.

Having assumed these conversations had become an expected part of design education, I was taken aback by how little the students cared. Instead, they were far more concerned with securing and keeping jobs in an increasingly precarious industry.

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience.

“How do you expect us to make any difference if this is how the industry works?” one asked. Another just wanted to know how to earn a living, without upsetting their employers.

Sources indicate that these were excellent questions, particularly as designers now compete with artificial intelligence capable of executing instructions at extraordinary speed. If design is reduced to following briefs and producing outputs, what space is there for a designer to effect any structural change?

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience. Designers are trained to solve problems, yet rarely encouraged to question who defined them, whose interests they serve, or whether they should exist at all. They are commissioned to make products more sustainable without questioning production volumes, or improve services without examining the policies that make them inaccessible.

Industry observers note that I often say design is a series of well-informed decisions. Every object, building and service emerges from decisions about resources, labor, budgets and the conditions of life.

According to recent reports, designers participate in these decisions, although they rarely control all of them. So where does their power begin and end?

Imagine a design studio commissioned by a city to address extreme heat in a low-income neighborhood. The brief requests solar-powered cooling shelters and shaded public spaces, with a fixed budget and deadline.

According to recent reports, during research, the designers discover that the proposed shelters would be too far from elderly residents most vulnerable to heat, while existing community centers could accommodate cooling facilities at a lower cost. What should they do? Follow the brief, collect their fees and pretend their hands are tied? Refuse the commission, leaving another studio to complete the work, perhaps feeling rebellious for a moment?

There is a third possibility. They could show the city why its proposal would fail to reach its intended beneficiaries and present an alternative within the same budget. Working with residents and community organizations, they could identify accessible locations, compare costs and demonstrate how the alternative better meets the city’s objectives.

The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Here we see a tangible expansion of design as a civic responsibility. Designers can use their expertise to bring communities into decisions that affect their lives, improving outcomes while sharing decision-making power.

And if the city insists on its original proposal? The client controls the budget. A junior designer acting alone may have little negotiating power.

Recent findings suggest that but a studio can incorporate community research into its contracts before work begins, negotiate a paid investigation phase and require the client to review evidence and alternatives before approving the design. Of course, this doesn’t guarantee agreement, but it makes critical inquiry a recognised part of the commission.

According to recent reports, design is a practice of applied imagination: understanding interconnected systems to intentionally shape the conditions of life. In this example, designers would examine the relationships between urban planning, public health, housing, energy and community governance. Their value lies partly in identifying what the original commission overlooked and developing viable possibilities with the people affected.

Thanks to the work of people like Victor Papanek, Tony Fry, Ezio Manzini and Arturo Escobar, by now it’s well understood that design has the capacity to shape the world but remains complicit in ecological and social destruction. The challenge today is to translate that knowledge into professional authority, economic leverage and meaningful participation in the decisions that will determine our collective futures.

Likewise, advocates of participatory design have long argued for involving people affected by design decisions. The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Meeting these challenges requires rethinking design education. Designers need to learn to investigate the historical conditions behind a problem, understand ecological and economic relationships, and work alongside communities to develop alternatives.

Design can shape community-owned infrastructure, food systems and forms of local governance as well as products and buildings. These are tangible fields of work requiring collaboration and shared authority.

We should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Of course, clients may refuse evidence, and insecure workers cannot always risk confrontation. Already there is too much pressure on Gen Z to save the world; we should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Studios, educators and commissioners must create paid roles and decision-making processes that give designers genuine influence. What if, for example, investigating the risks and assumptions behind a brief became an essential professional service, one that designers were commissioned and compensated to provide?

I keep thinking about those students at SVA, afraid of being considered difficult. We have taught them how to execute decisions without adequately preparing them to participate in making them. If designers are to take responsibility for their role in shaping the systems that govern our lives, they need a say in the decisions that produce those systems.

In the near future, success would mean residents gaining influence over where public money goes, with designers helping turn their priorities into lasting changes in public planning. This is design as a civic responsibility, and a meaningful distinction from machines optimized to execute instructions. To design possible futures, we must grow the agency designers hold, and the collective power they can help communities to build.

Industry observers note that céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian designer, artist, writer, educator and speaker based in Newly introduced York City, whose work focuses on climate problems and social justice. She is the founder of Slow Factory, a non-profit education and research platform that teaches about regenerative design. Her writing has appeared in The Cut, Vogue, Elle, Refinery29 and New York Magazine, among others. Her first book, A Woman Is a School, was published in 2024. Her upcoming book, Designing Possible Futures, explores the issues discussed in this article, and is due for publication in 2027.

According to recent reports, feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

It has been revealed that thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

In a recent development, drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Preparing for a Thai massage is simple!

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

In a recent development, your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.

Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.

However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.

What Ratti has revealed so far is that he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach to the event.

Specifically, he will use an AI assistant, aiming to challenge traditional approaches to developing exhibitions by highlighting emerging tools that can help curators.

“I am delighted to take on the direction of the Seoul Biennale and to explore the future of cities together with the Seoul Metropolitan Government,” indicates Carlo Ratti.

“Seoul is perhaps the best place in the world to ask how artificial intelligence and the collective wisdom of its citizens might shape the city together,” he continued.

“At the upcoming pre-biennale event, we will begin to introduce the people who will join us, and I think there will be a few surprises – one assistant curator isn’t even human!”.

Ratti is an Italian architect and engineer, and director of his eponymous studio Carlo Ratti Associati. He is also a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

He was appointed by Seoul mayor Oh Se Hoon, succeeding British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who curated the 2025 event.

Heatherwick centred the event on a long, four-storey-high wall displaying images that reflected the ideals of his Humanise campaign.

The Seoul Biennale was established in 2017 by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as a festival of international architecture and urbanism.

“The Seoul Biennale is a place where architects and citizens from around the world think together about the future of cities and explore new possibilities,” said mayor Oh.

“Together with general director Carlo Ratti, who has connected architecture, cities, and technology, we will prepare so that the sixth Seoul Biennale offers a new perspective on cities and architecture and a meaningful experience for citizens.”.

Ratti’s previous curatorial experience includes the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025, for which the theme was Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. It explored how architecture can be adapted to increasingly unstable living environments through cross-disciplinary collaboration.

At the time, Ratti noted, “Dezeen killed the traditional form of the biennale“.

The architect’s other recent projects include the French Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka and a proposal for a children’s hospital housed in a one-kilometre “green ring”.

Photography by Joas Souza.

UK studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region, a mixed-use office building in Lithuania designed as “a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking”.

Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the seven-storey Sąvaržėlė is located in central Vilnius, between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city’s commercial district.

The stacked building has a cantilevered design and houses office space, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe across its 19,000-square-metre space.

“At Sąvaržėlė, we wanted to create a workplace that extends into the city – one that welcomes people, encourages collaboration and contributes new public spaces to Vilnius,” RSHP associate director Jack Evans-Newton remarked.

“Occupying a unique position between the historic centre and the city’s emerging business district, the building brings these two identities together through a calm and contemporary architectural expression,” he continued.

“Clarity of form, generous public spaces and carefully crafted detailing create a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking, reflecting the ambition of a growing business district while respecting the scale and character of its historic setting.”.

Sąvaržėlė has large, adaptable floorplates, designed to create a flexible interior.

Recent findings suggest that the building has a stacked, rectangular shape and was made from prefabricated steel components that were bolted together on site. On the east and west facades, RSHP placed external ribs that the studio noted “echo the tones” of Vilnius’ historic architecture.

Sources indicate that sąvaržėlė is arranged around a central glass atrium with a striking yellow-lined elevator. It can be accessed via a number of different entrances that connect to the surrounding streets.

To enhance the building’s environmental performance, RSHP added a double-skin facade. This uses energy-efficient chilled beam cooling and automated natural ventilation to help reduce energy demand.

In addition, Sąvaržėlė has a 2,897-square-metre fully landscaped green roof.

RSHP has also recently designed a 45-storey skyscraper in Shenzhen and a curved-roof railway hub.

Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended).
  • But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s notable to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about upcoming plasma as an anti-aging elixir.
  • Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s notable to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about upcoming plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

In a recent development, “It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she states.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

Industry observers note that what that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”.

Sources indicate that about 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

According to recent reports, and the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

According to recent reports, “So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” indicates Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she says.

Part of the reason for this, notes Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”.

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

In a recent development, “I would call this a phase 1 study,” indicates Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”.

In a recent development, looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

It has been revealed that the nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.).

According to recent reports, nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Industry observers note that science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Recent findings suggest that almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

It has been revealed that older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Recent findings suggest that since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s notable to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

In a recent development, if you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:.

If you’re upcoming to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

It has been revealed that don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

💡 Key Takeaways
