📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

The Brussels-based studio is at the forefront of bio-regional and circular design, with a whole arm of its practice dedicated to the development of upcoming materials, often making use of construction waste.

Recently, the studio worked with UK studio Assemble and circular design lab Atelier Luma to create Le Magasin Électrique at Luma Arles in France, with a palette that included everything from rammed earth and construction waste to salt and algae.

Alongside these likeminded practitioners, BC Architects & Studies & Materials is at the forefront of a recent wave of interest in bio-based materials and vernacular methods – ideas that the studio has been championing for some 15 years, pushing for systemic change in the industry.

Founded between 2009 and 2012 by Ken De Cooman, Wes Degreef, Nicolas Coeckelberghs and Laurens Bekemans, the origins of BC Architects & Studies & Materials were – as its tripartite name suggests – not particularly conventional.

The studio is comprised of three different legal entities: BC Architects, an architecture cooperative; BC Studies, a non-profit “education laboratory”; and BC Materials, a material production co-operative.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s approach and outlook was borne out of a series of early projects in Burundi, Morocco and Ethiopia – where the studio briefly had a satellite office – which were grounded in working with local communities and materials.

It has been revealed that “A lot of our first experiences in architecture were linked to different construction cultures,” remarked De Cooman. “I lived in Ethiopia for five years, others were in Morocco for a long time, and at the same time, we were finding our way in Belgium.”.

It has been revealed that “It was a different path to learning architecture as a practitioner,” he continued. We learnt to work with local materials and short supply chains, to make do with what you find around.”.

The studio’s first built project was the Library of Muyinga in Burundi, developed using an open-source template from the OpenStructures network and constructed from compressed earth bricks alongside members of the local community.

It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials also designed several school buildings and a women’s shelter in Morocco, often using the construction process itself as an opportunity for the sharing of knowledge around vernacular construction techniques and materials.

According to De Cooman, however, this strand of the studio’s work was never intended to be long-term.

Challenging a tendency in the industry to view these methods and techniques as solely belonging to the realm of “humanitarian” architecture, BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s aim was to apply them to the business-as-usual processes of architecture and construction back home in Belgium.

“It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture,” remarked De Cooman.

“It was a huge learning process, and now we’re really focussing on the here and now because it’s here that we need to actually change the most.”.

While a big part of this change is the studio’s use of alternative materials, it was also based on the idea of building being an opportunity for shared learning, driven by BC’s belief in the the need for architects to be more engaged with the construction process.

We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other field.

Industry observers note that several of the studio’s early projects in Belgium the result of these learning workshops. Maison de Chasse, a rammed-earth hunting house, was constructed over the course of the first rammed earth workshop in Belgium, based on the techniques of Martin Rauch and Anna Heringer.

In 2017, the renovation of a series of warehouses in Ghent into an artist’s studio for Pascale Marthine Tayou was achieved via a five-week “Urban Construction Camp”, in which volunteers created a latest hempcrete structure inside an existing metal shell.

“We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other fields, not on paper, but with the heart and the hands included,” explained De Cooman.

“It is crazy that we now have a system where, as an architect, you draw all the execution files and send them to a contractor to execute it exactly how you drew it.”.

“The magic happens when everyone can get together – you can draw it together, find a passionate contractor to make it with.”.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials was keen, however, to not be defined by this smaller-scale work, with the whole point being to demonstrate how these techniques and materials could be scaled up into larger contexts.

The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to massive contractors and buildings.

A key means to achieving this was the formal establishing of BC Materials in 2018, enabled by the interest generated by their earlier projects. Alongside consultancy, workshops and training, the BC Materials arm also offers its own range of earth and clay products, Léém.

“The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings,” claims Wes Degreef.

“I think we were very surprised that the idea of working with a certain bioregion and its materials is something that we forgot in Europe.”.

According to recent reports, “Some of it still exists, but you really have to search for it. And with earth materials, for example, those crafts don’t exist anymore in Belgium. So we had to do it; we became the craftsmen.”.

Sure enough, the scale of the projects involving BC Architects & Studies & Materials – whether they are engaged as architects or as craftspeople – is growing.

“In the beginning, we were just like young, crazy people who are doing these weird things on Belgium,” mentioned De Cooman.

“There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.”.

In a recent development, there was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.

In Brussels, BC Architects & Studies & Materials worked alongside EVR-architecten to convert a former barracks into the Usquare Feder university district, the materials for which were sourced in part by the dismantling of several neighbouring buildings.

With numerous other residential and office projects in the works – including a upcoming bioregional materials hub and workspace in the centre of Brussels, Stadsatelierdeville, that will be its future office.

If it at times felt like BC Architects & Studies & Materials were up against the world, it is projects like La Magasin Électrique, which was a finalist for the 2026 Mies van Der Rohe Award, that reveal a growing international network who share their outlook, one that De Cooman is quick to credit with a lot of their own success.

“I think the dial is shifting, but I don’t think it is us who did it,” stated De Cooman.

“There are all kinds of practises, organisations, material developers, and so on, who see a different construction sector – it’s a wave, a societal shift.”.

“We’re very happy about it, but it’s broader than our practice. The construction sector is very conservative and we’re not there yet at all.”.

Degreef adds that external social and economic pressures have also had a hand in forcing change to some degree.

“After Covid and the impacts on material prices, the gap between contemporary materials and the materials we want to promote is not so significant anymore.”.

Asked if there is a particular type of building that represents a dream project, however, they remain resolutely focused on processes and systems.

It has been revealed that “I think, for us, it’s not in the buildings itself. It’s not what we build, but how we build and how everybody needs to build.”.

Recent findings suggest that to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

According to recent reports, your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:.

Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Sources indicate that regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

  • The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

Brussels‘ former Citroën Garage has been transformed into Kanal, a 40,000-square-metre museum for modern art and architecture with an exhibition programme developed with the Parisian art institution Centre Pompidou.

The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.

Claiming to be “Europe’s largest museum development”, Kanal – sometimes referred to as Kanal-Centre Pompidou – hopes to provide space for people to gather to enjoy visual art, performance, dance, music, film and architecture.

Opening to the public on 28 November, the canal-side building was originally built in 1934 as a garage and showroom for the car manufacturer Citroën.

Atelier Kanal aimed to keep the industrial character of the building by implementing a “light touch” approach, restoring most of the building fabric, repairing and upgrading parts where needed, and replacing other parts to improve climatic and acoustic conditions.

The garage’s former showroom, a modernist curved glass building with 20-metre-tall interiors, was converted into a gallery space topped with a publicly accessible rooftop.

“Rather than a spectacular gesture, our proposal offers an attitude of ‘radical optimism’ – open and non-prescriptive, spontaneous and instinctive – much like the spirit of modern progress in which it was created,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The interior is a fine example of elegant industrial engineering, while the glass facades clearly express early modernism,” it continued.

“Our ambition has been to trust the building as we found it, embracing its industrial character and many layers of use.”.

Three newly introduced buildings were added inside the existing structure, including a four-storey volume with a basement level that contains art galleries, and another volume housing a 378-seat auditorium and the Kanal offices.

The third volume is the new home for Brussels’ museum and archive of architecture, Kanal Architecture, which was formerly known as CIVA.

Rising nine stories on the north-east side of the campus, across from the art galleries, the structure includes exhibition spaces, a library, archives, research centre, bookshop and workshop spaces.

Architecture collective Assemble designed an indoor playground on the first floor of the museum, which features playscapes informed by volcanoes, planets, and piles of coal that were once transported on the canal.

Elsewhere in the building are a library, bookshop, rooftop bar, restaurants and an in-house bakery.

Kanal’s year-round programme of exhibitions was developed in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou art museum in Paris.

“Kanal invites citizens, organisations, collectives and communities to appropriate and inhabit large parts of the building, for production, performances, events, informal gatherings or simply to spend time,” noted Atelier Kanal.

Industry observers note that “The museum extends beyond curated art, becoming part of the city and its fabric,” it continued. “In this sense, Kanal departs from the traditional museum and instead offers a place for civic gathering, responding to the growing absence of shared public spaces in our cities today.”.

Other museums that have recently opened in historic buildings include the London Museum, located in a transformed Victorian market building, and a bank in Santander that was transformed into the Faro Santander museum.

Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners swiftly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

In a recent development, dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Industry observers note that locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Industry observers note that have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

In a recent development, it might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”.

Recent findings suggest that whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

It has been revealed that also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

Industry observers note that FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Industry observers note that following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Design agency Base Design has created a more compact version of credit card manufacturer Visa’s logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a newly introduced typeface, as part of a refresh of the brand’s visual identity.

While the 2021 Visa wordmark remains unchanged, the refresh included creating a shortened symbol for the brand, rolling out the latest Visa Sans typeface, and creating a blocky hero graphic to market towards a younger generation.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition – it’s relevance,” remarked Base Design executive creative director Min Lew.

“Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”.

In a recent development, as part of this strategy, the studio cut the V out of the existing wordmark to function as its own symbol. It will be used on credit cards and appear across digital platforms.

The studio also wrapped it in colourful bar, which will also be used on graphic elements such as posters, and to frame text.

“More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity,” mentioned Lew.

“This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences.”.

For Visa Sans, Base Design and Displaay Type Foundry also based the design on the existing logo.

The typeface features rounded edges akin to the rounded corner of the Visa V, and overall, extends “the logo’s character across the wider identity”.

Ultimately, the upcoming identity was created to be used across different smaller, touchpoints according to the team, such as at tap-to-pay stations, at checkout, or online, as the brand appears “for only a moment” in day to day life.

Recent findings suggest that “We have deep trust and recognition as a brand,” mentioned Visa chief marketing officer Frank Cooper III. “This refresh gives us an opportunity to build on that.”.

A more subtle approach to logo and branding updates has been popular in recent years, such as at Walmart and Google.

In contrast, the US restaurant chain Cracker Barrel recently took a hard swing at a logo patch, which was immediately met with online backlash and promptly scrapped in favour of the original design.

#172998. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 18 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1051 w)

Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 18 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” says Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, says Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

Recent findings suggest that an allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

In a recent development, by contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

According to recent reports, if you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication before pollen counts rise. That's because antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller claims. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller notes to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran states. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

According to recent reports, sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller states. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

Industry observers note that if you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Daniel Reiser.

The UK’s Royal Society for Arts has announced five Royal Designers for Industry, who include Durrell Bishop and Bridget Baines, as well as naming an Honorary Royal Designer as it celebrates its 90th anniversary.

The awards, which were established in 1936, recognise outstanding talent across landscape architecture, technology, illustration, fashion and theatre. They are given by Royal Society for Arts (RSA) and can only be held by 200 designers at any one time.

This year’s winners are product and interaction designer Bishop, multidisciplinary designer Harris Elliott, illustrator Laura Carlin, costume designer Tahra Zafar and landscape architect Bridget Baines.

Baines co-founded international practice Gross Max, and her fellow Gross Max founder Eelco Hooftman (pictured in main image with Baines) was given the Honorary Royal Designer award this year.

The winners were chosen for their “joyful” designs,.

It has been revealed that “Ninety years on, the Royal Designers are still looking forward,” Keeper of the Faculty of Royal Designers for Industry Johanna Gibbons remarked. “This year’s appointments show how far design now reaches, from public landscapes and picture books to exhibitions, the stage and the objects we use every day.”.

It has been revealed that “Their work is joyful, and it is serious about making life better,” she continued. “That is what unites Royal Designers across the decades: a living entanglement of disciplines that, with the RSA Fellowship, is a profound force for good.”.

Last year’s winners included designer Yinka Ilori and journalist Mona Chalabi, and the award has also been given to designers including Es Devlin, Vivienne Westwood, James Dyson and Zandra Rhodes.

According to the RSA, the winners represent the “sheer breadth of design today”.

“Great design changes how we experience the world, often in ways we barely notice,” RSA programme manager Catherine Joyce.

“For 90 years, Royal Designers have shown what extraordinary creativity can achieve, and how it can make life better for everyone,” she continued.“These six appointments are a wonderful reminder of the sheer breadth of design today.”.

Dezeen also recently celebrated the best designers of this year as part of our Dezeen Awards, including Ilori, Yasmine Ghoniem and Keiji Ashizawa.

Photography by Daniel Reiser.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.
  • Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down.
  • Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Recent findings suggest that spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Sources indicate that are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Recent findings suggest that have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

Sources indicate that when your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Industry observers note that have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a substantial part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Sources indicate that some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

It has been revealed that for infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Industry observers note that another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

Recent findings suggest that if the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels rapidly through the digestive system.

Industry observers note that while liver complications can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

It has been revealed that dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

In a recent development, while green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Spanish lighting brand Marset has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice.

Marset‘s selection includes the Gambosa table lamp, created by designer Mathias Hahn to reinterpret the classic shade, stem and base as one smooth, glossy sculpture in steel and opal polycarbonate.

In a recent development, gambosa is defined by its elegant composition, with a round-ended body that looks as if precariously balanced. It also features a considered cable design that sweeps down one side of the lamp like a signature.

It is distinguished by its select palette of colours, with combinations of orange, moss grey, black, pale pink and opal that evoke mid-century style combined with contemporary curation.

With the Lauro collection, Marset has revived a genuine 1970s design classic from its own catalogue, featuring chunky tubes of bent steel.

It has been revealed that created by designers P Aragay and J Pérez Mateo, the Lauro lighting comes in table, floor and wall variants. According to Marset, the range represents the technical achievements of a time when bending steel was a huge challenge.

Another of the highlights from Marset is the Ringo lighting, crafted by designer Joan Gaspar from transparent polycarbonate that is rotomoulded, giving it a dimpled texture reminiscent of a melting block of ice.

Available in flush-mounted or pendant styles, the design has a simple cylindrical shape, with scale and materiality bringing fresh life and visual impact.

Another of Gaspar’s designs is Domus, an angular bollard-style outdoor light that, through simple gesture, recalls a warmly lit house at night.

It has been revealed that the design is available in three heights. Units can be optionally combined to create a sculptural look and the illusion of multiple windows.

Geometric glass volumes, metal detailing and glowing bar-shaped lighting elements meet in the Fragile collection, designed for the brand by Jaume Ramírez.

The lights come in pendant, wall and table formats, each made up of spherical and conical shades that lend them a playful aesthetic.

The roots of the Marset brand stretch back to the 1940s, when Francisco “Paco” Marset established a small metal foundry in Barcelona.

His grandchildren Javier and Carlos Marset helped reposition the organization as the global design brand it is today when they took over in the 1990s, bringing on board designers such as Gaspar, who is a frequent collaborator.

  • Named the Edinburgh Futures Institute, the project involved refurbishing the Category A-listed structure, originally designed by Scottish architect David Bryce, and integrating upcoming teaching and work spaces for the University of Edinburgh.
  • The Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) mentioned the award jury praised the project for its “modern, welcoming, clever and stimulating” design that successfully blends “Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Video by Jim Stephenson.

An old Victorian infirmary transformed into an educational space by UK studio Bennetts Associates has won the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland for 2026.

Named the Edinburgh Futures Institute, the project involved refurbishing the Category A-listed structure, originally designed by Scottish architect David Bryce, and integrating upcoming teaching and work spaces for the University of Edinburgh.

The Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) mentioned the award jury praised the project for its “modern, welcoming, clever and stimulating” design that successfully blends “Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation”.

“The Edinburgh Futures Institute stood out for its civic generosity, scale and ambition,” said RIAS president Libby Heathcote, who is associate director at Reiach and Hall Architects.

“Balancing loyalty to David Bryce’s diagram with creativity in introducing bold new interventions is a remarkable achievement, blending historic Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation,” she continued.

“The result is a modern, welcoming, clever, and stimulating place that people want to work in and return to.”.

Central to Bennetts Associates‘ redevelopment was the restoration of the building’s existing fabric, which was at risk of dereliction after being vacated in 2003.

Updates to the existing structure included reopening an original clock tower and public plaza, as well as the restoration of original wards and 150-metre-long corridors.

Across its five floors, flexible teaching and work zones were added alongside fresh public areas such as exhibition space and a 450-seat event hall below ground.

The Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual prize named after Scottish architect Andrew Doolan, who passed away in 2004. It recognises buildings of all typologies.

The Edinburgh Futures Institute was chosen as this year’s winner ahead of two other adaptive reuse projects. These have each been featured in a series of videos produced by Jim Stephenson and published by Dezeen and RIAS to showcase the shortlist.

The other two projects shortlisted were the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by London-based Studio Octopi and the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture.

Previous winners of the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland award include the Union Terrace Gardens by Stallan-Brand and LDA Design and the Burrell Collection museum by John McAslan + Partners.

Video by Jim Stephenson.

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the major three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:.

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she states.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”.

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina indicates.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:.

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most notable planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s vital to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she notes it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

In a recent development, “The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina notes.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is notable, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

Industry observers note that to find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

  • As the Vitra Design Museum hosts Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses, the first major retrospective of the Sri Lankan architect in over 20 years, co-curator Johan Deurell explains why the ‘tropical modernist’ label has confused Bawa’s legacy.
  • Geoffrey Bawa is one of Asia’s most prolific 20th-century architects, known for projects such as the Bentota Beach Hotel, the Kandalama Hotel and his own houses, Number 11 and Lunuganga.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography is by Iwan Baan unless otherwise indicated.

As the Vitra Design Museum hosts Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses, the first major retrospective of the Sri Lankan architect in over 20 years, co-curator Johan Deurell explains why the ‘tropical modernist’ label has confused Bawa’s legacy.

Geoffrey Bawa is one of Asia’s most prolific 20th-century architects, known for projects such as the Bentota Beach Hotel, the Kandalama Hotel and his own houses, Number 11 and Lunuganga.

Bawa’s work is often described as tropical modernist, as it is seen to blend Western modernist principles with Sri Lankan vernacular traditions and materials.

But Deurell remarked he and his co-curators deliberately stayed away from this label, which was coined by Western architects and scholars and is closely associated with British colonialism.

“We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism,” he told Dezeen.

Industry observers note that “It comes with so much baggage. But it’s also not the most useful tool to discuss Geoffrey Bawa’s work with.”.

As one of the Vitra Design Museum’s in-house curators, Deurell oversaw the show with Shayari de Silva, chief curator for the Geoffrey Bawa Trust, and Ikko Yokoyama, a senior curator at M+ in Hong Kong.

The exhibition offers a broader understanding of Bawa’s legacy, highlighting qualities that set him apart from the modernists.

For instance, it highlights how his buildings worked with existing landscape conditions.

“He built with nature rather than against it,” Deurell noted.

“Modernist site planning often involved clearing the land, rather than having buildings like Kandalama Hotel, which snakes its way around a rift.”.

The show also spotlights the sustainability of Bawa’s designs, in terms of both ecology and socioeconomics.

His buildings harnessed the skills of local craftspeople and were built with locally sourced materials. They also featured climate-conscious strategies for shading and ventilation.

This approach is particularly relevant today, said Deurell, as the building industry faces the reality of a climate crisis.

“His ideas on landscape and ecology was really at the forefront,” the curator said. “He had a holistic approach to architecture and he built with nature in mind.”.

Sources indicate that the exhibition features a scenography designed by Lina Ghotmeh, who was named Dezeen Awards’ Architect of the Year 2026. It contains over 250 exhibits, including drawings, models, archive photography and furniture.

Among the highlights is a new photography series by Iwan Baan, capturing 11 of Bawa’s buildings as never seen before.

Drone photography offers a look at Bawa’s Number 11 house and University of Ruhuna from above, while other shots show people occupying the Lighthouse Hotel and Bentota Beach Hotel.

Furniture on show includes a mix of original Bawa designs and versions of well-known modernist pieces remade with local materials.

In a recent development, as Deurell explains, these were not intended as copies. The originals were not available in Sri Lanka at that time, so Bawa simply commissioned replicas for use in his interiors.

Standouts include a version of the Barcelona Chair by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, with a welded iron frame and stripy upholstery fabric designed by Sri Lankan designer Barbara Sansoni.

“Bawa collaborated with artists throughout his career, ” said Deurell, pointing to long-standing collaborations with Ena de Silva and Laki Senanayake as well as Sansoni.

“All of these artists ran their practices as social enterprises, so they would employ villagers and train them in a craft,” stated the curator. “It highlights the social consciousness within his practice.”.

It has been revealed that drawings bring another dimension to the exhibition. Highly detailed maps, floor looks and sectional drawings emphasise the relationship between building and landscape.

Although these drawings were mostly produced after the buildings were completed, they offer an insight into the architect’s mindset.

Deurell points to a quote by Bawa, where he talks about landscape elements as being part of “the total picture”.

“They are just as key as the architecture itself”, he said.

All archive material is courtesy of Geoffrey Bawa and Lunuganga Trusts.

In a recent development, geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses is on show at the Vitra Design Museum in Weil am Rhein, Germany, from 26 September 2026 to 28 February 2027, before a run at M+ in Hong Kong from June 2027. An architectural intervention is not simply a question of how much or how little to introduce, but of understanding precisely where and how to act. This precision begins with a careful reading of the existing context, including the recognition of the spatial, material, and environmental conditions that shape a place. It extends into the process of design and construction, where complex considerations are distilled into deliberate, coherent decisions. Rather than pursuing formal complexity or reduction for its own sake, a measured intervention seeks to establish a meaningful relationship between what already exists and what architecture can contribute.

Artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for next year’s Brit Awards trophy, a silver sculpture covered in holes to “expose the interior of the statue”.

Since 1992, a different creative has been selected to design the handheld trophy for the UK music industry’s annual Brit Awards.

Essex-born Whiteread has designed the statuette for next February’s ceremony, which is her interpretation of the annual trophy depicting Britannia, a helmeted warrior that is a traditional symbol of Britain.

The result is a minimalist silver statuette cast in resin and covered in holes to draw attention to the inside of the trophy.

“I exposed the interior of the statue, as an artist would do with their music,” remarked Whiteread.

Whiteread then handpainted the nickel-plated trophy in a silver hue.

The artist is known for casting everyday architectural forms, such as staircases or sheds, in materials including plaster and concrete to showcase their negative space.

She explained that when designing the Brit Award, she wanted to put her own spin on the recognisable trophy.

“I saw this as a natural extension of my work – to continue to celebrate and recognise British art and creativity,” said Whiteread.

Recent findings suggest that “Art and culture are under very real threat,” she continued. “So I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists, whether from music or the visual arts.”.

The Brit Awards will take place on 27 February 2027 at the Populous-designed Co-op Live arena in Manchester, where the ceremony was held for the first time at the start of this year.

To mark the awards’ departure from London, where it was held consecutively before 2026, British fashion designer Matthew Williamson designed an amber trophy to reference Manchester’s worker bee city logo.

Other former trophy designers have included British architect Zaha Hadid and British-Indian artist Anish Kapoor.

Photography by Brit Awards.

Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that cutting back on calories but not losing weight?
  • Recent findings suggest that everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight.
  • It has been revealed that the concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”.

Recent findings suggest that everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

It has been revealed that the concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research demonstrates starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

In a recent development, evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

Sources indicate that what does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:.

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

Industry observers note that however, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

In a recent development, most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

In a recent development, so what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

Industry observers note that first, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Sources indicate that choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Sources indicate that weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That remarked, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

It has been revealed that despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

#172980. Industry News: Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1446 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1446 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism.
  • According to recent reports, the truth?
  • Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

According to recent reports, the truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

In short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, indicates Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

It has been revealed that that mentioned, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research shows that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Recent findings suggest that every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

According to recent reports, this can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Recent findings suggest that strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

Recent findings suggest that by strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison claims what’s most important is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

In a recent development, protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

According to recent reports, protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

However, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, states doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

For most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That mentioned, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

In a recent development, an often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of challenges, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research shows that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

According to recent reports, there is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:.

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:.

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

Hawkins\Brown's temporary housing for homeless families in London is a UK first

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London, the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK.
  • Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.
  • Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Fred Howarth.

Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London, the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK.

Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.

Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.

Intending to set a benchmark for temporary family housing in the UK, Hawkins\Brown aimed to create a welcoming building that eases the stress of families facing homelessness.

“Many of the families who come here are fleeing hugely painful domestic situations,” said Hawkins\Brown partner Nick Gaskell.

“The Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre aims to make a traumatic period a little more bearable by providing a caring, calming and uplifting environment for as long as they need it.”.

Designed to be in keeping with the neighbouring buildings, the exterior of the U-shaped building is lined with striped bands of orange-toned bricks and pops of pale green metal sheeting.

A secure, landscaped courtyard with play space at the centre of the building helps bring natural light into the surrounding flats.

Inside, the apartments were designed to offer higher-quality living arrangements than typical temporary housing, with tall windows, underfloor heating and open-plan kitchen, living and dining rooms.

Community and family support spaces on the ground floor of the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre include a reception, visitor breakout areas, children’s indoor play spaces, communal laundries and staff facilities.

Based on the studio’s research into dementia-friendly design, Hawkins\Brown used colour zoning, visual landmarks, accessible graphics and high-contrast colours in the centre, aiming to make the space easy to navigate for residents and visitors of all ages and abilities.

Elsewhere in London, architecture studio HTA Design recently unveiled what it says is the largest upcoming-build council housing development in the UK.

In Ukraine, architecture studio Office for Future is working on plans to transform a school into temporary housing for families affected by the war in the country.

Photography by Fred Howarth.
